subtopic: EFFECT OF ICE CONDITIONS ON LOBSTER FISHERY- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
EFFECT OF ICE CONDITIONS ON LOBSTER FISHERY- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgency. Extreme ice conditions in many lobster fishing districts in the Atlantic region have already meant a delay in executing this fishery. The persistence of this condition will result in shortening the season to the point of loss of livelihood to many hundreds of fishermen who are dependent on this fishery. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That the Minister of Fisheries give immediate consideration to extending the lobster season in those areas affected.

1.	Has the Food and Drug Directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare established a bio-availability standard for all drugs prescribed by physicians across Canada and, if so, is this bio-availability standard mandatory to all prescribed drugs?
2.	What percentage, if any, does this bio-availability standard require and does this standard percentage apply to all drugs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
1. The Health Protection Branch has established a guideline for the bioavailability of drug products which it assesses in its current programs on drug quality. Bioavailability tests are not at present mandatory, although there is provision in the Food and Drugs Act and Regulations to demand proof of efficacy. The whole field of bioavailability is very much in the development stage, with the clinical significance of bioavailability data still not fully understood. In order to put this problem in proper perspective, we have commissioned an advisory committee of non-governmental medical experts to consider all aspects of it, and report within the next few months.
2.	The guideline specifies a minimum bioavailability of 80 per cent for the product, relative to a reference standard. It has been applied to drugs chosen for reason of critical medical use, high sales volume, narrow therapeutic index, possibility of contaminants, and unknown problems with bioavailability.

WELFARE ASSISTANCE TO CHILDREN AGED 16 AND 17
speechtext:
1.	Are children aged 16 and 17 able to obtain welfare or any other form of social assistance that would enable them to live independent of their name and, if so, on what basis?
2.	(a) What are the statistics of children (i) 16 (ii) 17 receiving assistance as in Part 1 by month for the years 1970, 1971, 1972 (b) if these figures are not available, for what reason and are any actions planned to secure such information?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: WELFARE ASSISTANCE TO CHILDREN AGED 16 AND 17
speechtext:
1. Children 16 and 17 years of age may be granted social assistance in every province. However, the legislation governing eligibility and the rates of assistance paid vary from province to province. Under the Canada Assistance Plan, the federal government may share in the cost of such assistance granted on the basis of a needs test which takes into account an applicant's basic requirements and the income and resources available to him. A summary of the provincial situation follows: In Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, persons 16 years of age and over may be granted social assistance. In most cases the provincial legislation requires that the possibility of family support be investigated, and that the young person register for employment or provide documentation attesting to school attendance or to the desirability of continuing at school. In Newfoundland and Saskatchewan persons 16 years of age and over who have established themselves as self-supporting may be granted assistance. In Manitoba, assistance to persons under 18 is provided on a non-ward basis by the child welfare authority. Quebec does not grant social assistance to persons under 18 except on an emergency basis. Exceptions are made for young people who must live away from home to receive medical treatment or educational courses not covered by Manpower training programs. In Alberta young people over 16 who are not attending school are usually considered responsible for their own support; but emergency social assistance may be provided when they are unable to obtain employment. Applicants for social assistance who are 16 and 17 years old may be provided with ward or non-ward care through the child welfare program. Young people are generally not required to return to a home situation which has been investigated and found unsatisfactory.
2. (a) Provincial governments are responsible for the administration of social assistance programs, and statistical data reported by them do not identify recipients of social assistance by single-year age groups. Hence, it is not possible to answer this enquiry at this time, (b) An Information System Team is presently engaged in a project which has as its central focus the design and development of a system for gathering and processing such statistical data.

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT-SPEED LIMITS FOR LARGE VESSELS
speechtext: Has the Department of Transport established speed limits for large vessels using the main boat channel between Prescott, Ontario and Kingston, Ontario and, if so (a) what are the limits in specific areas (b) how are these limits enforced and by whom (c) what plans does the Department have for the strictest possible enforcement during the year 1973 in order to prevent damage to shoreline property by excessive waves?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT-SPEED LIMITS FOR LARGE VESSELS
speechtext:
In so far
as The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority is concerned: The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, together with the Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation, have established speed limits for the main channel between Prescott and Kingston for all commercial vessels in excess of forty feet in overall length. These limits have been in effect since June 1, 1970 and are as follows: (a) Prescott to Blind Bay Vi mile east of Light 162, 15 miles per hour; Blind Bay Vi mile east of Light 162 to Deer Island Light 186, 13 miles per hour; Deer Island Light 186 to Bartlett Point Light 227, 10 miles per hour upbound, 12 miles per hour downbound; Bartlett Point Light 227 to Tibbetts Point, 15 miles per hour, (b) Limits are enforced by both Seaway entities.

The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority carries out speed surveillance throughout the Lake St. Francis-Blind Bay area. This surveillance is carried out with the help of radar equipment. Locations are selected at random and checks are carried out on a 24-hour basis. The Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation is responsible for speed surveillance in the area from Blind Bay to Tibbetts Point, (c) Recognizing the high water level situation in the upper St. Lawrence River area, the Seaway entities introduced temporary speed restrictions on March 27, 1973 in the following areas: Ogden Island Buoy 99 to Blind Bay, from 15 miles per hour to 14 miles per hour; Bartlett Point Light 227 to Tibbetts Point, from 15 miles per hour to 13 miles per hour. Agreement has been reached between the two entities for further temporary speed reductions from Tibbetts Point on Lake Ontario to Lancaster on Lake St. Francis when the level of Lake Ontario reaches a critical point. The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority plans to continue its speed enforcement program with particular emphasis being given to sensitive areas. Random radar surveillance will be carried out in all speed restricted areas both during night and daytime hours, including holidays and weekends.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
that Bill C-176, to amend the Criminal Code, the Crown Liability Act and the Official Secrets Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of Bill C-176 is of very great importance. It is a subject matter that has been before this House of Commons on two separate occasions. This afternoon I want to address myself very briefly to hon. members here about its content, doing so with the earnest hope that the broad measure of agreement, which I am sure there is in the House about the importance of this matter and the need to make these changes in the law, will result in the expeditious movement of this bill to the committee, back to the House and into effect as the law of Canada.
One of the problems we have experienced in the past with legislation is that too much kindness and too much talk about the merits of legislation has resulted in a delay in the implementation of important measures. This bill is important because it recognizes in a formal way the importance of privacy in our Canadian life. I say "in a formal way" because of course privacy has been recognized in indirect ways through various parts and parcels of the law over the years. But in this bill, for the first time at a federal level, the right of privacy is recognized expressly in a protection of privacy act. We are all familiar with the deepfelt belief that privacy and individuality are of fundamental importance to our own democratic way of life. With the growth of electronic devices which make it possible to hear or intercept conversations and communications without awareness of that interception by the persons participating in the conversation, we have
Protection of Privacy
had an increase in the problem of protection of privacy and an increase of the problem of the security of the people in this country, as well as their ability to converse with the knowledge that it is a private matter and not one which is being overseen or overheard by other persons.
The bill attempts to protect the right of privacy, I believe in a number of effective ways. It makes it a criminal offence to engage in this interception and a criminal offence with significant potential penalties attached, one of which is imprisonment of up to five years. It makes it an offence to possess or to sell devices of the electro-magnetic type or other devices which may be used for such interception purposes. Again, it places in the law significant penalties of up to two years imprisonment for this sale or possession of these devices. There is, of course, provision for the proper and authorized possession and sale but in a limited way, a way which is necessary for other portions of the bill. The bill also places a limitation on the communication of information if it is obtained in an illegal way. It proscribes that and also creates the potential of damages, punitive damages, to be assessed against those who improperly obtain or communicate information with electro-magnetic or other similar devices. That is the main thrust of the bill. It sets up the protection of privacy and the importance of our ability to communicate with one another without being surreptious-ly overheard or having our conversations intercepted.
The bill puts in play, I think, effective measures to ensure that that cannot be done and that that will be hereafter, after the passage of this bill into law, an illegal matter and therefore one which we can attempt to restrain with the full power of law enforcement. The bill on the other hand, recognizes the potential desirability of the use of these devices on occasion in the public interest, in the public cause, when our enforcement officers, either for security reasons or reasons associated with offences where other measures may fail, need these devices and will find them useful in the enforcement of the general law and order on our society. In the case of criminal matters, the bill proposes the authorization of such uses by persons engaged in the enforcement procedures. The bill accepts the conclusion of the House committee in 1970, which was supported by the House again in committee in 1972, that these authorizations should be obtained from a judge, a judge defined, as the committee chose in the 1972 session, to include superior court, county court and district court judges. The Solicitor General, in the case of certain federal matters, and the provincial attor-neys-general in the case of provincial matters, are involved in the applications for these authorizations and therefore are seen as having a direct responsibility for this.
There is, in a sense, a double protection through the responsibility of the Solicitor General or the provincial attorneys general and the actual authorization of the use of the warrant by the judge. That is one of the issues which has been the cause of some discussion and controversy. It may again be a matter upon which the committee will wish to focus some attention. I hope when we get to that stage we will look at it seriously once more, but not to the point of preventing the bill becoming, at an early date, a part of the law of the land.

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
It has been argued in the committee that, on the one hand, it might be better if the full responsibility for these authorizations were placed upon the Solicitor General or the attorneys-general as the case may be. The involvement of the judge, I think, is a useful precaution, even though it is recognized that in an ex parte proceeding he is faced with material being presented to him upon which he must make a judgment without having necessarily the total part of the argument which an opponent might put forward to him. It is none the less a useful precaution I believe in ensuring that the form of the use of electronic device is in fact apparently on a sound basis.
The bill itself sets out that these are not to be first-rank techniques of investigation but rather in the way of additional, fail-back or substitute ways of investigating when more ordinary means of investigation fail. There is further political protection in the requirement of report by the Solicitor General or by the provincial attorneys-general each year with regard to the number and types of uses of devices in the course of enforcement within their areas of jurisdiction. These, I think, are the interesting and useful balances. It will be argued before the House I am sure-and we have a good deal of knowledge about the arguments which may be made in the committee because of the appearance of this matter before the House on two separate occasions and the appearance of witnesses before House committees-that the bill, even as it stands, is perhaps a little too restrictive in respect of the investigative powers, in the shortness of the period for which warrants may be issued and in the exact terminology of the type of cases for which they may be applied.
I will be eager to hear hon. members views once again in the committee as we look at the exact and precise details of the legislation. There also has been some controversy in respect of the proposals in the bill to exclude evidence in criminal or civil matters under federal jurisdiction which had been obtained in an illegal or unauthorized manner following the enactment of this bill into law. There, we would be seeing the introduction into our law I believe for the first time of an exclusionary rule which I think is, in its history, merely intended to add a further sanction against the illegal obtaining of evidence on the theory that it will not so readily be obtained as evidence if it is not admissible in a subsequent case. I think it is worth noting that there are significant other sanctions in the bill before us, including both the penal provisions and the civil or punitive damages provisions, including Crown liability if any Crown servants are involved in an illegal interception. The committee may want to consider further whether this exclusionary rule is reasonable or necessary in this particular case with these additional sanctions.
There is, in addition to the sanction argument, the issue which will be before the committee of whether it is right for a court to be involved with evidence which is illegally obtained or, on the other hand, whether it is fair or decent to the administration of justice to see a cause unresolved because certain clear evidence is not before the court because of the technical rule excluding it.
I think these are important points, and I hope and look forward to having the committee conduct further discussion upon them, but not in a way which will obscure the 
main and fundamental thrust of the bill upon which there was agreement in the committee of the House of Commons when the main portions of this bill were put forward in almost the same form as they now stand, as well as in the committee of the House in 1972 when a bill very much like Bill C-176 was before it. That main thrust is to make it an offence to engage in electronic, electro-magnetic and similar eavesdropping or interception of conversations to protect privacy in a fundamental way by the creation of that offence, and then only to allow certain very narrow exceptions to that main point. With the passing of the law, therefore, the interception of communications by private citizens, whether for purposes of trade or curiosity, will be a criminal offence. We will have the possibility of restraining such activity and, perhaps even more important, of adding to the assurance of individuals that their privacy is protected and that they do not have to fear that such devices are around them.
In addition to the prohibition of the use of these devices we have also the prohibition of their possession and sale, again except in very narrow categories. That is the main thrust of the bill. It is an important addition to the Criminal Code and to the law of the land and I, therefore, urge hon. members to help in the swift passage of the legislation, even though we must debate in committee the interesting points to which I referred and resolve them there. While they are important, they are not as important as the main thrust of the bill which, I hope, will soon be a part of the law of the land.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES

Mr. Speaker, the shortness of the speech of the minister makes it somewhat difficult for the rest of us to comment on a seminal piece of legislation-if I could use that term-but I am afraid that, although the official opposition will want to co-operate in the passage of this bill, there will be three or four speakers from this side at least who will want to have a chance to make their comments before the bill reaches the committee.
I think I am conscious of the fact that we must not be like the pharisees and thank God that we are not like other men when we consider this bill in juxtaposition to the grubby and sordid events which are called the Watergate scandal in the United States. However, it must be admitted that the Watergate scandal makes an interesting backdrop for a public debate in this country. It is my submission that, although the events of Watergate could have taken place here legally until this bill is passed, there is no question that their ethics would leave a great deal to be desired.
One of the major problems connected with this bill for spokesmen for the official opposition such as me is not really in the thrust which has been discussed by the minister regarding the protection of privacy, with certain narrow exceptions, but rather-and I will comment briefly on this and hope that perhaps somebody else from the government will allay my concern about it, and then I will consider some other aspects of the bill-in the rather loose, use of certain words, if I can say so fairly, in clause 6 on page 21 of Bill C-176. There is a description in the clause of espionage and sabotage, and the following are the words which I think are used much too loosely, certainly for this party's acceptance, namely: " .. . or any
May 7, 1973

other subversive activity directed against Canada . . This is not the language of the Criminal Code. This phrase is nowhere defined, either in the Criminal Code, or in this bill, and I hope that the committee will direct itself, first of all, to getting rid of such loose language or, second, to to at least defining it.
We must remember that we are within three years of the imposition of the War Measures Act, and I think that put all of us as parliamentarians-I am not being partisan at all-on our guard when we see rather ill defined language about what is or what is not subversive activity. As I have said in other contexts, one man's draft dodger is another man's hero, and I think that in defining the right to privacy and in defining peculiar ways in which the government can listen in on conversations-and I think this bill is a positive measure-we must be very careful that we are not busy listening in on activities which, although they may not be very pleasant for governments or for administrations, none the less are in no way part of what we might call the scandalous activities of espionage and sabotage.
That is just a comment, but I hope the government will want to tighten up this language, and if not tighten it up, remove it altogether because sabotage and subversion are well defined. There is a law concerning them but nowhere in this statute or the Code is there anything about any other subversive activity directed against Canada. This needs to be defined, and I hope the government will see to it that it occurs.
The problem of the control of electronic means of surveillance has become acute due to rapid technological advances which now offer comprehensive techniques for bugging and snooping. As is obvious, telephones can be tapped, offices bugged, files photographed, movements monitored, and communications recorded without the knowledge of the person involved. I think the minister will agree that science and technology have-until this bill is passed-outstripped the legal means of controlling technology. This is really what we are about. The law is finally catching up with technological change. As I said when I started, it is appropriate for us to be discussing this subject while the evils of Watergate take up so much of the news these days. The assumption that Watergate could not have happened in Canada is naive, I think, and dangerous, particularly because, until now no federal law has existed concerning wiretapping and other forms of electronic eavesdropping.
As the minister has said, the aim of the bill is to make a crime of the wilful interception of a private communication. To repeat what the minister said-if I may flatter him in this way-the central question is the delicate one of how far you can restrict law enforcement officers without interfering with them, how much you have to restrict them in order to give better assurance that there is, in fact, protection of privacy in the bill. The bill prescribes a particular kind of compromise in this area. If protection is to have meaning, all methods and devices for wire tapping and electronic surveillance must be controlled.
The Task Force on Privacy and Computers-if I may say so gratuitously, one of the more interesting recent
Protection of Privacy
government publications-explains the privacy of the person as "aimed essentially at maintaining the dignity of the human person. Our persons are protected not so much against the physical search as against the indignity of the search, its invasion of the person in a moral sense." The right to privacy is not absolute. "In any society, claims to privacy are continually balanced against other values and interests by social, political and legal processes. The security and welfare of the collectivity and its institutions are values which tend to prevail over individual claims to privacy." Of course, what the government is seeking, and I hope it thinks it is seeking it with our help, is to try to strike a just balance between public protection and safety and the protection of privacy. As the minister pointed out, this question has been considered several times in recent years.
The Justice and Legal Affairs Committee studied the matter of electronic eavesdropping and made a report on March 11, 1970. The committee listed 20 major recommendations. Among them were that wire tapping, electronic eavesdropping and industrial espionage should become crimes. Also recommended by the committee were well defined limits on police use of electronic bugs, a list of crimes justifying such investigation, application for use by an attorney-general and authorization by a judge, a stated time period for surveillance, and a yearly report to parliament by the attorney-general. I am glad to say that many of these recommendations have been incorporated in the bill that we are now considering. As I have said, at present there are no privacy laws at the federal level in Canada. British Columbia and Manitoba have privacy laws for civil actions, and I am informed that several provinces have legislation concerning interception of telephonic communication.
This bill is the third bill concerning wiretapping and electronic eavesdropping introduced by the government. When the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) was minister of justice he introduced a bill on privacy on June 28, 1971. That bill died on the order paper after first reading. Then, there was Bill C-6 on the same subject. It was given first reading on February 21, 1972. I think it is worth noting, and anyway I am going to note it because others may read that there is this chronology available. I always have a horror that some day others will read these words, but if so, no doubt thay will be interested to know what happened. Hence the excuse for the history lesson, Mr. Speaker. On May 2, 1972, Bill C-6 was given second reading, and was discussed in committee in early June. The bill, with amendments, was reported back to the House on June 14, and we know what happened then. It did not get any further, and once again died on the order paper.
The present bill has been before us for just a month. It was given first reading on April 13. Essentially, Mr. Speaker, it is the same as Bill C-6, with one or two amendments suggested by the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Outlawed is wilfully listening in or recording of a private conversation by electromagnetic, accoustic or mechanical devices. It will become a criminal offence to possess, sell or purchase any device that is primarily useful for invading privacy.

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
Information gained from illegal wiretapping would also become an offence punishable by imprisonment. The bill authorizes monitoring aimed at preventing and detecting subversive or criminal activity where other investigative procedures are judged not likely to be successful. Evidence obtained as the result of information acquired though illegal wiretapping can be used in certain circumstances. Bugging must be authorized by a provincial attorney general or by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). Application must be made to a Superior Court judge, and bugging can be approved for a 30 day period, with the right to apply for an extension. In case of emergency, the approval of a judge is not required for authorization but the permit is valid for only 36 hours, and approval of a judge is necessary if the evidence obtained is to be used in court.
Basic to the consideration of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is the recognition of the right to know. In a moment I am going to quote the distinguished hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, the present Minister of Finance, who made a very interesting and now, I am afraid, forgotten by many, speech in September, 1969.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-176 takes centre stage at this critical time in political democracy. Canadians have been exposed to and some have experienced the results of wiretapping and electronic surveillance. We have witnessed and read the revelations of the Watergate affair and are shocked by the conduct and cover-up of persons in high places. Mr. Speaker, Watergate is now making the McCarthyism period in the United States look like the age of reason. When we learn that the late J. Edgar Hoover, as head of the FBI, considered Martin Luther King a subversive and a liar and applied electronic surveillance to Dr. King, it makes us realize the restrictions that must be placed on electronic surveillance.
We in the New Democratic Party support the principles of Bill C-176 but are concerned with some of the procedures and provisions in it. I notice that the former minister of justice is here, Mr. Speaker. I read his speech and some of his interviews in which he indicated that there should have been consultation between the Minister of Justice and the attorneys-general of the provinces. I hope that procedure was followed prior to the framing of this bill because he indicated the necessity of uniformity in the law and that the power to license the manufacture of electronic equipment probably lay within the provincial
Protection of Privacy
jurisdiction and that such licensing was necessary. I hope this course has been adopted by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) and that he will be able to respond to that assertion.
In view of the fact that there is now virtually no legislation limiting electronic surveillance, this bill provides a good starting point to deal with this serious problem. Prior to this legislation all we had was one federal statute which made it an offence to interfere with any of the property of the Bell Telephone Company, to work on its lines or intercept any message transmitted thereon, as well as a few provincial statutes which made it an offence to divulge the contents of a conversation heard by means of wiretapping, except when authorized or directed. These restrictions were completely unsatisfactory and provided an opportunity for wiretapping by many people and groups. Probably the worst offenders, Mr. Speaker, were the police forces of this country.
Wiretapping and electronic surveillance have increased in use and sophistication at a rapid rate in the past few years. They have become the tyrant of technology and have taken on different forms and types, pressing into the privacy of man's conversation and into his home. We have had electronic snoops with regard to criminals; we have had electronic snoops with regard to car salesmen, where a manager has had electronic surveillance of conversations with customers; we have had electronic surveillance with regard to union activities; we have had data bank information revealed, and in some cases that has been unwarranted and unjustified; we have had psychological surveillance by way of truth serums; we have had corporate espionage and now political espionage as exemplified in the affairs of our neighbours to the south.
This bill deals with some of these areas but certainly not all. Probably the most important is the danger of the misuse of data bank information and there is a need to protect individuals and businessmen against the misuse of information about them which is sorted in computers or data banks. There is now a provincial or international flow of information through the telecommunications facilities, linking computers with central data banks. This is certainly not covered by the bill.
This legislation is clear in three aspects however: first, electronic surveillance in the private sector is completely illegal; second, the possession, sale and purchase of electronic equipment by unauthorized persons which render it primarily useful for surreptitious interruption of private communication is illegal and, third, civil liability of persons connected with illegal wiretaps is established. These measures are welcome.
The major concerns of the New Democratic Party are first, the issuing of permits by judges; second, the admissibility of certain evidence from illegal wiretaps and, third, amendments to the Official Secrets Act concerning the issue of warrants by the Solicitor General for alleged espionage and subversive activities. These are the three main areas. I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) will deal with them when he replies, and also at the committee stage.

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
The general rule that private wiretaps are illegal is subject to this main exception: That the police are permitted to make wiretaps, provided they have complied with certain criteria satisfactory to the judge before a permit is issued. That brings into sharp focus the question of personal privacy in a democratic country and underlines the problems arising from the tyranny of technology. I submit that personal privacy is central to man's dignity and liberty, and to deny him this privacy may be to undermine his very humanity and erode belief in our democratic institutions and the judicial process. In the words of Mr. Justice Field of the United States:
-Of all the rights of the citizen, few are of greater importance or more essential to his peace and happiness than the right of personal security and that involves, not merely protection of his person from assault but exemption of his private affairs-from the inspection and scrutiny of others. Without the enjoyment of this right, all others would lose their value.
This proposition was restated by Professor Edward Ryan at the Couchiching Conference of August 5, 1971 when he said:
The right to privacy, far from being a mere individual claim, is itself a public interest of the highest order, in which may be found the wellsprings of individual creativity and group expression which are at the heart of popular government. They cannot be allowed to be imperilled. No more fundamental laws to our ideals is possible than that posed by the possession and potential abuse of overly wide governmental powers in this area.
From those statements arise such questions as: Should the police be given the power to snoop, and is wiretapping necessary and effective in combatting crime? Many have said that the police should be in the same position and as well equipped as criminals with respect to the use of electronic equipment. This bill deals with the question of private surveillance and private surveillance is made illegal, as is the possession, sale and purchase of unauthorized electronic equipment.
The second assertion that crime is on the increase does not necessarily jibe with the facts. The fact is that more crime is reported today than in the past, and therefore it does not follow that more crime is being committed. The assertion that police wiretapping and electronic surveillance is necessary to combat crime should be reviewed on the basis of facts. The self-conferred right to wiretap by the police has had no appreciable effect on crime detection. Actually, the evidence discloses that wiretapping is used by the police for the purpose of aiding in investigation and seldom if ever for the purpose of collecting evidence. The following was said in the brief of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association which was presented to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs:
In a learned law review article, Brown and Peer made the following observation, generally supported by experts in the field: 'Wiretapping is of very little use in connection with ordinary felonies and crimes of violence. There is lacking in this sporadic sort of crime the pattern of continuity necessary for effective wiretap operation by the police officers.'
No less an authority than Ramsay Clark, U.S. President Johnson's last Attorney-General, voiced the same misgivings when he said:

In several cities where organized crime is most severe, police and prosecution have in the past used wiretap without inhibition. It has not been effective. Organized crime still flourishes in these communities. In other cities where there has never been organized crime, police have never used wiretap. The massive programs required to end organized crime have no place for wiretap. It is too slow, too costly, too ineffective .. . Organized crime cannot exist where criminal justice agencies are not at least neutralized and probably corrupted to some degree . .. The F.B.I. used electronic surveillance in the organized crime area from at least the late 1950's until July 1965 ... So far as is known not one conviction resulted from any of the these bugs ... In 1967 and 1968, without the use of any electronic surveillance, F.B.I. convictions of organized crime and racketeering figures were several times higher than during any year before 1965. The bugs weren't necessary.
With regard to organized crime in Canada, we had a royal commission studying crime in Ontario in 1961. In their report they said that organized crime was virtually non-existent in Canada. In 1969 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police stated that organized crime in Canada was in its infancy. We must, therefore, ask whether it is necessary in the circumstances to give the police such wide powers in these fields. What worries the members of my party, Mr. Speaker, is the procedure that will be adopted with regard to permit applications to a superior court judge. Such applications will be made ex parte by way of affidavit, and the procedure will involve an application to a superior court judge. When there is an ex parte application, there is a one-sided type of justice. The decision is made on the basis of an affidavit prepared by a police officer, in most instances, and there is no right to cross-examination, which is contrary to our adversary system. The judge will need to make a decision on the basis of an application made by one person or group of persons.
In the United States, especially in the state of New York, they have had the experience of police officers who wanted to make application for wiretapping permits going judge shopping. In other words, they have gone to judges who were sympathetic and who have issued permits on evidence that was very scanty. I do not think that this will happen in Canada. Certainly, it is not in keeping with our concepts of Canadian justice. We think that all parties should be represented in court. We think the adversary system is necessary and we think that examination, cross-examination, legal argument and judgment should be part of our system. All these factors are most important, but yet are missing when a police officer applies to a judge on an ex parte basis.
The bill also provides for a private communication, intercepted without authorization, to be not admissible as evidence, but that information or things disclosed as a result of unauthorized interception may be admitted as evidence. In other words, the direct evidence is inadmissible, but the derived evidence may be admissible. We are departing from the usual rule which states that all relevant evidence is admissible, regardless of how it is obtained. It has been suggested that the rule should be that the evidence should be admitted only it does not offend the fundamental concepts inherent in our ideas of ordered liberty under the law. We should consider whether it is reasonable evidence, whether it is just evidence and whether it is in accordance with the Bill of Rights before it is admitted in court. Surely, there could be a voir dire to determine this issue.
May 7, 1973

It has been indicated that most police wiretapping is not designed to gather evidence, but to gather information from which evidence can be developed. Professor Beck of Osgoode Hall put it into sharp focus when he said:
The only real control over the police is self-control. To achieve self-control over illegal wiretapping the law should provide that all charges arising from illegal wiretapping must be dismissed in court. This would have a magic effect in assuring that whatever wiretapping legislation is passed by Parliament, it will in fact be obeyed by the police.
I think the members of the New Democratic Party agree with the sentiments contained in that statement by Professor Beck.
Perhaps the most frightening parts of the bill deal with the amendments to the Official Secrets Act. All the safeguards relating to police wiretapping disappear. I quote: The Solicitor General of Canada may issue a warrant authorizing the interception or seizure of any communication if he is satisfied by evidence on oath that
(a)	the purpose of such interception or seizure is related to the prevention or detection of espionage, sabotage or any other subversive activity directed against Canada or detrimental to the security of Canada; and
(b)	such interception or seizure is necessary in the public interest.
A provision follows that under which the application for the warrant is made by an officer of the RCMP. The warrant is issued by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). The accounting procedure, the report aspect, is, and I quote:
The Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police shall from time to time make a report to the Solicitor General of Canada with respect to each warrant issued pursuant to subsection (2) setting forth particulars of the manner in which the warrant was used and the results, if any, obtained from such use.
In other words, all the safeguards which we have applied to the police in general do not apply to the Solicitor General or to the RCMP when the wiretapping is for the purpose of prevention or detection of espionage, sabotage or any other subversive activity. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is long overdue. Finally, the arduous efforts of many law reformers to provide a meaningful form of protection of privacy in Canada are about to be rewarded. This is not to say that I support all the provisions of this bill before us, but merely to indicate that I support wholeheartedly its general legislative thrust as a valuable and necessary reform to an area of law which until recently was largely ignored in Canada.
In my remarks I will outline, in general terms, some objections to some of the specific provisions of the bill with the hope that the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs will entertain appropriate amendments following second reading with the same constructive and non-partisan approach that the committee followed in its proceedings during the 28th parliament. However, the minister and hon. members will be only too aware that this is a new parliament, with many new members having new or different ideas. Under no circumstances will the opposition necessarily feel bound by the proceedings taken under Bill C-6 in the 28th parliament when this government had a majority in the House and in the committee. Indeed, it is my hope that the end product of our labours here and in committee might reflect improved protections against invasion of privacy and further limitations on authorized interceptions than are in the present bill.
To put my jurisprudential premise at its simplest, I believe that in a free society the right to privacy should be protected by law and that there should be derogations from this protection only where public need is clearly demonstrated by those who seek to use means to invade privacy in a rational way for the public good. The onus should always be on those invading privacy, not on those seeking the legal protection of the right.
Compared with the United States and the United Kingdom, Canada got off to a relatively late start in this field. However, in the past five years, a great deal of ground has been covered. I refer not only to the hard work of the
3478

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
many able and responsible members from all parties who participated in the work of the standing committee in the last parliament, the initiative of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) when he was Minister of Justice, or to the continued interest and open-mindedness of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). Of equal importance, I refer to the pioneering work of the Ontario Law Reform Commission in 1968, with its now famous study and report on protection of privacy in Ontario, which laid much of the groundwork for the subsequent activities of the standing committee at the federal level and the resulting initiatives of the government. The Ontario study was prepared largely by my friend and former colleague, Edward Ryan, who was quoted so ably by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), who later became counsel to the federal standing committee and assisted in the preparation of its report which forms the basis of the bill before us. Mr. Ryan and members of the Ontario Law Reform Commission certainly deserve a share of the credit for the bill we have before us today. Canadians will always be in their debt.
However, the concerns which precipitated the interest of law reformers five years ago are much greater today. Canadians should know that technological advances have led to the production of bugging and photographic devices which permit a man's every movement or word to be recorded without his knowing about it. Canadians should also be aware that it is now a relatively simple matter for telephones to be tapped, offices to be bugged, files to be photographed, physical movements to be monitored and communications to be recorded. Yet until this bill is passed, there is virtually no right of recourse or protection in law against this sort of activity. Indeed, had the type of bugging activity which took place during the Watergate affair last year taken place in Canada there would have been absolutely no legal recourse against the perpetrators of this heinous conduct. Unlike the United States law, Canadian law provides no constitutional right to privacy. However, in the context of today's society I would submit that erosions of privacy of the kind I have mentioned, certainly in the political context, constitute the beginning of the end of political freedom as we know it in this country.
The bill before us goes a long way toward providing the protection which Canadians want and need. For the first time, wiretapping is made a crime, punishable by way of indictment and liability to imprisonment for a five-year term. Second, the exceptions are specifically defined, the most important being the carefully-defined authorization of wiretapping carried out by law enforcement officials acting under the instructions of the Attorneys-General of the provinces or the Solicitor General, or their agents specially designated in writing. The bill makes a bold attempt to rationalize, structure and confine the method of requesting an authorization and the person who can give the authorization. However, I have grave reservations as to the specific method proposed in the bill particularly its reliance on the judiciary to provide ultimate authorization, as opposed to the Solicitor General or the Attorneys-General. I shall elaborate on this point later.

Third, the bill provides another valuable protection by making possession, sale or purchase of bugging devices an indictable offence, subject again to certain clearly-defined exceptions in the public interest. Also, the bill makes provision for the forfeiture of such devices in cases in which a person has been convicted of wilful interception or unlawful possession. Another important feature of the bill is that it creates the offence of disclosure of information obtained by unlawful wiretapping or bugging.
Perhaps one of the most innovative aspects of the bill is the introduction of the concept of civil damages, both punitive and actual, in situations of unlawful interception or user disclosure. This means that a person whose privacy has been invaded in this fashion not only has criminal sanctions at his disposal but can proceed against those responsible to recover a monetary amount equivalent to the actual damage to his reputation, and also punitive damages to the extent of $5,000. This may prove to be an important additional deterrent to anyone contemplating illegal invasions of privacy of the kind under consideration.
Unfortunately, though, the bill fails to provide any means by which a person whose wire has been tapped by public officials can find out that his privacy had been invaded in this fashion. There is no provision requiring the Solicitor General, the Attorney-General or their authorized agents to notify the person subject to a wiretap even after an investigation has been completed.
As a practical matter, therefore, it will be very difficult, if not impossible, for a person to seek the prosecution of a public official, or to claim damages against him under the suggested changes to the Crown Liability Act. The present draft seems to be based on the premise that what a man doesn't know won't hurt him.
It is significant that the standing committee in its 1970 report recommended that notification be made within a reasonable time by registered letter, subject to reasonable exceptions where there is a continuing investigation or where the wiretaps are related to espionage or sabotage on behalf of a foreign power. At the very last, the bill should require that in the annual report of the Solicitor General or of the Attorneys General an accounting be made of the number of people who were not informed following the completion of the wiretap investigations surrounding their cases.
I support wholeheartedly the elaborate annual reporting requirement of the Solicitor General and the Attorneys General in this Bill. If invasions of privacy are to be authorized in accordance with the mechanisms proposed, it is absolutely essential that the responsible political officers account to the public for the number of times and the circumstances under which they have initiated wiretapping, and give some indication of the extent to which wiretapping has been successful or unsuccessful as a means of law enforcement. Any Solicitor General or Attorney-General who has been over-zealous in his use of such techniques will obviously be directed toward his rightful place by the force of opposition scrutiny, press vigilance and public opinion. While it is good that these annual reports are required to be tabled or made public "as soon as possible after the end of each year", I would
May 7, 1973

like to see the insertion of a more specific time limit of not more than six months after year end. The unfortunate practices of the present government with respect to the filing of annual reports are surely evidence of the need for further protection. Also, the Solicitor General's report should include information as to the number of persons to whom he issues licences each year to lawfully possess bugging devices which are otherwise illegal.
The public accountability aspects of the bill bring to mind what is perhaps the most reprehensible provision before us, one which allows the Solicitor General to drive a truck right through even the reporting safeguard. I refer to the provision which allows a Solicitor General to issue a secret warrant authorizing the interception of communications if he is satisfied that the purpose is "related to the prevention or detection of espionage, sabotage or any other subversive activity directed against Canada or detrimental to the security of Canada." There is no reporting requirement respecting these secret warrants. All that is required is that the Commissioner of the RCMP report from time to time to the Solicitor General; other than that these secret warrants will never see the light of day.
In any event, what does the term "any other subversive activity" mean? Clearly, it means whatever the Solicitor General wants it to mean. Anything that varies from the status quo could be swept into the net under this elastic formula, whether it be taking a trip to Mainland China or reading the wrong kind of books or knowing the wrong kind of people, as defined by the Solicitor General. We need only contemplate the experience in the United States during the Red scare and deportations of the early twenties, the Red scare of the McCarthy era in the fifties, their disastrous Asian tragedy of the sixties in Viet Nam and the Pentagon papers revelations of the seventies, all of which resulted from the abuse of secret powers directed against subversive activity, to know how dangerous is this provision in the bill before us. The Solicitor General need not even apply to a judge for the issue of these warrants. He does not even report to parliament about his use of these absolute powers of secret surveillance. He need not state how many times he has exercised these powers.

I believe the statement you have made is correct.
The standing committee of the twenty-eighth parliament recognized the need for a strong power to guard against subversive activities. But the committee also recognized that parliament must be kept informed in order that it might assess the propriety of the use of the power which it grants and the effectiveness of the safeguards, so
Protection of Privacy
as to maintain vigilance in preventing the erosion of civil liberties. Yet this government has persisted in maintaining the same sort of secrecy that so characterized its methods of operation during the October crisis of 1970 when civil liberties were reduced to one of the lowest levels in Canadian history. Surely, something is wrong in the state of Canada at the present time if this is allowed to remain in the bill.
At the very minimum, parliament must be informed of the number of times the Solicitor General sees fit to use this dangerous power. Secret surveillance of the sort contemplated by this section has no place in a free and democratic society.
There is another glaring inconsistency in this bill, already referred to by the hon. member for Broadview, relating to the evidentiary provisions as to admissibility. This bill as drafted would preclude direct evidence obtained by illegal wiretapping from being admitted in court proceedings against the originator of the communication intercepted, but it would allow the fruits of such illegally obtained evidence to be admitted, that is the evidence obtained directly or indirectly as a result of information acquired by such illegal interception. In my view, this is totally inconsistent with any rational application of the exclusionary rules of evidence, no matter what the jurisdiction. Either you admit all evidence from illegal wiretapping or you exclude it all.
To exclude it is to admit that such a rule of evidence is necessary in order to control the behaviour of police and public officials in their use of wiretapping. To admit all such evidence, whether direct or indirect, is to leave to the discretion of the court the weighing of such evidence as to its relevance in the context of the case before it. But the legislation as it now stands contains a serious analytical defect. My own preference would be to exclude both direct and indirect evidence which has been obtained by illegal wiretaps, and I was encouraged to note that such an amendment was proposed following second reading by the standing committee of the last parliament and was narrowly defeated by a vote of six to five. Hopefully, this matter will be given serious reconsideration once again.
No further proof of the futility of the present provision is required than to refer to the evidence of the chief of police of Toronto on behalf of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police before the standing committee, there he indicated that in some 155 cases of wiretapping leading to criminal prosecutions in the courts in Toronto, in not one instance was the actual intercepted conversation used in prosecutions, but only the indirect evidence which was obtained as a result of having received that conversation. Clearly, the present evidentiary protection in the bill is totally illusory.
Perhaps the most debated aspect of this bill when it was before the last parliament and in committee was whether the final authorization for wiretapping by the police and public officials should be given by a judge, or by the Solicitor General or the Attorneys-General or persons designated by them. After much debate and division of opinion, the committee opted for the final authority to be given by a judge of a superior court of criminal jurisdic-
26314-3}

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
tion, but only after the request for authorization was initiated by the Attorney General, the Solicitor General or persons specially designated by them. Later the committee went on to broaden the range of judges who could provide this type of authorization. Included were all county and district court judges in Canada and all provincial court judges or judges of the sessions of the peace in the province of Quebec. I believe the term used in the legislation is "a judge as defined in Section 482 of the Criminal Code".
In my opinion, it was a mistake not to vest the final authority in those political officers who the public hold responsible for the conduct of the government in this country. It should be the Solicitor General or the Attorneys General who have the final say. The exercise of the power to grant authority to invade privacy can affect the critical balance between the government and people. Surely, then, the people must be able to hold a responsible minister to account for his use of the power. Under this bill, the minister can take shelter behind the judge's decision.
The bill provides that the Solicitor General, the Attorney General or agents designated by them will apply to a judge in a secret ex parte hearing for authorization to wiretap. In most cases it will be the agent applying, not the Solicitor General or the Attorney General. One can expect that most agents to be named would be justices of the peace, Crown Attorneys or even chiefs of police. In any event, all of the records of the application are sealed. Surely, this is a blatant abuse of the traditional judicial process. Secret ex parte hearings have no place in our judicial tradition, and they can place a judge in a very difficult and embarrassing position. This may well undermine the traditional function of our judiciary. The judges will have no data to go on other than a written accusation or statement of suspicion by the agent. They will not know both sides of the story and they are not allowed to weigh both sides. In other words, they are not judging; they are being told to make the minister's decision for him. Responsible police officials told the standing committee that they did not want to go to judges. They wanted the Solicitor General or the Attorney-General to take the responsibility, as he should under our parliamentary system. The idea of using a judge, I am told, is borrowed from the United States, and the experience there, as the hon. member for Broadview has pointed out, has been a sorry one.
A New York District Attorney noted recently that the police in his state seemed to know which judges required strict proof and which judges were to be avoided. Throughout Canada, there are 255 Supreme Court and Superior Court judges, 181 county and district court judges, and close to 200 provincial court judges in Quebec, well over 600 in all, who would be qualified to authorize wiretapping under this bill. There is no reason to believe that a similar type of judge shopping would not take place here. As one who prefers greater restrictions on authorized wiretapping, I would strongly urge the committee and this House to give reconsideration to vesting ultimate authority in the political officials, and not the judges.
A final concern with this bill is that the range of the offences for which wiretapping may be authorized by a

judge may be unnecessarily broad. The standing committee proposed that the use of this power to lawfully intercept communications be limited to 19 extremely grave crimes, including the control of syndicated crime. Eighteen of the 19 offences listed by the committee carry possible penalties of 10 years or more in prison. This bill before us will allow the police to seek authorization to intercept communications in the case of any indictable offence. In other words, the extraordinary power of invasion of privacy could well become a routine investigative tool and, contrary to the recommendations of the standing committee, wiretapping could be used on such matters as petty theft, income tax evasion, impaired driving, the possession of marijuana and theft over and under $50. While I would not for a moment condone any of these offences or attempt to impair the attempts of law enforcement officials to arrest and convict people committing them, I would seriously question whether authorizing wiretapping for such matters is not really the equivalent of using a shotgun where a rifle would do.
In the same vein, I think that the demand of the Association of Chiefs of Police to extend wiretapping to summary conviction offences is an example of unnecessary and dangerous overreaching of law enforcement goals at the expense of civil liberties of the public generally. I sincerely hope that the committee will avoid this broad shotgun approach.
As one last matter, I want to express some reservation about the provision in the present bill permitting emergency permits to wiretap to be granted for up to 36 hours by an agent designated by the Solicitor General or the Attorney-General without the necessity of having to go before a judge. My fear is that in some provinces the use of such emergency permits may become more the rule than the exception, unless the Attorney General there takes an extremely firm position against such a practice. My own preference, if emergency permits must be part of the legislation, would be to require authorization by the Attorney-General or the Solicitor General personally. Otherwise, the bulk of authorized wiretapping activities may consist of 36-hour taps approved and then revoked by the local agents in each case. These are difficult to detect except ultimately through the Attorney General's annual report to be made public each year, but always after the event.
In closing, may I say that this is one of the most significant pieces of legislation to come before this House this session. It is to the minister's credit that he responded to the pressure applied by the opposition in committee last month and promptly came forward with this bill before Canada is faced with a situation similar to Watergate, with no legislative sanctions to remedy it.
