speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to compliment the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) for what I regard as one of the very best speeches I have heard in this House. I have only been here since 1968, but it is one of the best speeches I have heard on the very important question of human liberty and the related subject of human privacy. I think it was an excellent speech. The question with which we are faced with respect to this bill really is part of the larger
May 7, 1973

question of what limits if any are to be placed on human privacy. That question is a root question, a philosophical question, which must be faced by any society at any time in history. It is a question, however, which democratic societies are inclined to think they need not deal with because democracies, as forms of government, ttiink they are not liable to the problem of the invasion of privacy associated with other types of regimes.
I find it unfortunate, in a sense, that this debate in this House at this time in the history of North America should in fact have aroused such little interest from the point of view of attendance in the House. I realize there are important matters which must be attended to and with which members have to deal. However, I think the attendance here is indicative of the attitude of many people, including Members of Parliament, toward the question of privacy and toward the question of human liberty itself. There is a basic assumption, so prevalent in our land as well as in others, that one need not be concerned about the question of a human right until one is hit personally or until one's group is hit. Then, there is a psychological response.
I suggest that the specific matter with which we are dealing now is one which could open up in a fundamental way the question of the invasion of privacy on the kind of systematic basis that was alluded to by the previous speaker; and in such a way in terms of its long-range consequence for Canadians that all of us in this House, if we cannot be here physically for this debate, should take great care in reading the debate and of course in looking at the bill with which we are dealing before we cast a final vote. Privacy is essential to individuality itself. It is fundamentally important to what is known as the integrity of the personality. This is a notion philosophically as old as the Greek philosophers and medieval theologians and as recent as the intellectual concern of the 20th century psychoanalysts. People as diverse as Plato, J. S. Mill, Bertrand Russell and Sigmund Freud have all recognized that without a sense of privacy, without a distinction between public concern, public involvement, community concern and community involvement on the one hand and the basic right in other instances to have privacy in one's life, that without this distinction being legitimatized and institutionalized in society what you really end up with is the abolition of individuality in people, the abolition of freedom and the abolition of creativity in the human 'being.
I try to avoid rhetoric as frequently as possible in my speeches and avoid exaggeration, but I think this type of issue is of just this importance. If we take steps in terms of the laws of this parliament which lead to the systematic invasion of privacy, we are really taking steps which can lead to the systematic elimination of the individuality in people. For the purpose of the debate, I define the right of privacy as the recognition of the legitimacy of man's right to think, to speak and to meet with people under circumstances from which all others but those whom he himself has selected are excluded. That, as I say, is privacy. As I have said, I see this as being essential to human individuality.
To state the opposite circumstance I think illustrates the case. That is, if we have a state in which no privacy is permitted, liberty and creativity are also non-existent. The
Protection of Privacy
most recent, in terms of the 20th century, standard works of art one cites for this are, of course, the works of Kafka and, in the English language, Huxley's "Brave New World" and George Orwell's "1984". The book "1984" I remind hon. members is a novel written by a man in this century who was responding not, as is frequently thought, simply to capital "C" communism but indeed to the possibility of any totalitarian society which has at its disposal the technological means of the total elimination of privacy. It has at its disposal the possibility, therefore, of the total control of the individual. I think the elimination of privacy, as I said a minute ago, leads clearly in that type of direction. The danger is that, as Canadians, we tend to associate that kind of danger simply with the Nazi regime with which Germany and western Europe had to live in the 1930's and until the mid-1940's. Or we think of Stalinist Russia as another form of totalitarianism.
However, the phenomenon of the threat of privacy is not to be restricted to those countries in those parts of the world. In my view, the United States at the present time is undergoing, in terms of its own internal life, its most significant crisis perhaps of this century as a democratic society. The United States now has the technology to totally invade the privacy of all her citizens virtually any time of the day or night. Not only that, but we are witnessing in what people all over the world have called "that great democracy," the United States, the fact that technology can be used by a democratically elected president, or if he has not authorized it directly himself it is clear that it has been used by officials appointed by him and directly responsible to him.
The point I am making is that in the United States there is the systematic use of modern, technologically sophisticated devices for the total invasion of people's privacy and hence of their freedom, and that is taking place not in a totalitarian society but in a democratic one. It is taking place in part-and this is an important point to make in the context of the central weakness of this bill which is to be found in clause 6 which gives such extraordinary powers to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), totally unimpeded by normal judicial processes-in a democratic country in the form of what is now known as the Watergate affair. It is taking place, I would argue, in part because the men and women who were directing the operation believed in the legitimacy of what they were doing. As de Toqueville said in the last century, and since by a number of other serious commentators, but de Toqueville was the first observer of mass democracy, he saw then the dangers of a democratic society using instruments or devices, because they believed in the overwhelming legitimacy of their case and had majority support, which other kinds of governments in previous times would have been reluctant to use.
The point is that in a democracy, precisely because we mobilize public support for causes, precisely because there is a danger that once you have the majority on your side you might point to those who disagree with that majority as being the enemy, as being in a sense alien, there is a danger of using the full support of a democratic majority to attack the roots of human freedom, namely the right to privacy. I, for one, believe that a lot of people

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
acting under the orders of President Nixon, or-and I hope this turns out to be the case-under the orders of senior officials appointed by him, believe that it was right to spy on Senator McGovern, that it was right to violate the basic legal rights of Mr. Ellsberg, that it was right to engage in undermining the political processes because they believed that a man named McGovern was last year undermining the democratic objectives which the regime of the time was trying to further.
The point I am trying to make is that many of the Nixon officials did not believe that they were doing evil. They believed that Mr. McGovern somehow, instead of bringing peace for which he was working, was going to bring in a kind of society which was the very contradiction of what they thought was in the spirit of the basic American principles of democracy. As I see it, as a democrat in a democratic country, this is the kind of broader issue with which we should be concerning ourselves in this kind of debate. When we give, for example, under the provisions of clause 6 of the bill, the authority to the Solicitor General to use all the modern devices such as wiretapping to invade the privacy of individuals and of groups without going, at least initially, through the judicial route of applying to a superior court judge for a warrant or without having to consult any other person, I would argue that we are leaving ourselves open to the kind of situation which occurred in the United States. I stress the words "in principle", and I do not mean of course that the present Solicitor General or the present government would deliberately embark on such action.
I wish to repeat the point I was making a minute ago about democratic societies. I am convinced that a majority of the members of the U.S. Congress, if this debate were taking place in that chamber a year and a half ago, would have thought it inconceivable in principle that the systematic corruption which is now being revealed by the investigations of the Watergate affair could take place. The point, then, is that if we are going to justify, under certain extreme circumstances, the invasion of privacy, then we have to take extreme precautions in terms of the procedures that will be used by a democratically elected politician in so acting. I suggest that it is a glaring and unacceptable weakness of this bill that the Solicitor General can, relying on his own definition presumably, decide what is going to be defined as a "subversive activity directed against Canada", which is the wording in this bill. This can lead to the kind of thinking by certain eminent politicians in the United States which clearly enabled them psychologically, in a country which is now at the centre of world history, to perceive themselves as being profoundly threatened, not only from without but from within, and to use measures which we find totally unacceptable.
Therefore, to guard against that eventuality in Canada, I think that the minimum we need in terms of implementing the provisions of this part of the act is a safeguard provision that would make it mandatory, at the very least, that the Solicitor General obtain a warrant from a superior court judge and, beyond that, that he must provide to this parliament on a regular basis a full and documented report on all the instances in a given period when action has been taken under the provisions of clause 6 of this bill. If such a change is not made in the bill, judging from

what the previous speakers from the Conservative and NDP groups have been saying, I am sure that we will not get this bill passed at all. I hope that the minister is listening with care to what hon. members are saying in this debate if he wants to get it passed.
There are two good provisions in the bill, and we join in praising the minister and his predecessor for prohibiting under this bill private wiretapping and the sale, possession or purchase of equipment to be used for that kind of activity. These are good provisions, but I have entered what I regard as a very important caveat. We expect a change in the provisions of clause 6 which enable the Solicitor General to act in much too sweeping a manner.
I want to conclude with a recent instance, not from American, German or Russian history, but one which occurred in Canada. About three weeks ago a conference was held in this city, Ottawa, organized by the Canadian Society for Industrial Security. It was a three day affair attended by representatives of Northern Electric, Comin-co, International Harvester, Bell Telephone, Eaton's and a number of others. The ostensible purpose of it was to discuss security. We do not know what aspects of security because we were excluded from this conference by a group of Canadian businessmen who held it here in the capital city.
* (1640)
I went down to the conference. I was told that the assistant-commissioner of the RCMP, H. C. Draper, was to deliver a paper entitled, "The Threat from Subversive Elements." I was told that he was going to deal with subversive elements in the trade unions. As a Canadian and Member of Parliament, I thought it would be interesting to hear what an assistant-commissioner of the RCMP was going to say about Canadian workers to a group of businessmen. But when I got there I was barred entry. I was told that this was a security matter. I ask what kind of security matter it was. What right did the RCMP have to collect information on Canadians from one coast to the other, information which if revealed or spoken about outside this chamber would probably be subject to the laws of libel? And what right does a state police official, a senior one at that, have to divulge information of that kind about one group of Canadians to another group of Canadians? In this instance, I am told that it was about a group of Canadian workers in the trade union movement, and it was to be divulged to a group who usually are on the other side of the bargaining table, a group of businessmen who will be confronting the workers at different times when negotiating employment contracts. What can justify such action?
After this issue was raised in the House of Commons, I was pleased that the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) informed me that there will be no more such conferences. But, Mr. Speaker, this body has met each year for the past number of years. This body of businessmen has been concerned ostensibly with security matters. It is little known in Canada. It is little talked about. The conference was interesting, not only in terms of the papers delivered but in terms of the literature that was made available, advertising courses which representatives of the companies could take. The literature included brochures from a certain institution in the United States inviting represent-
May 7, 1973

atives of business companies to go there and learn all about bugging, to learn all about listening devices, to learn all about means of, in effect, spying on Canadians who work in offices and factories.
What I am concerned about in this context is that a national police force, the RCMP, should have had a spokesman at that conference, speaking about one group in our country and disclosing what, if used in a different context, could conceivably amount to libellous statements. There is no place in our society for our national police force to perform that kind of act. Little concern has been expressed about that matter by the average person, or by the Canadian newspapers. At times I am at a loss to understand the lack of concern about individual rights that is so widespread in our country. Little concern is expressed about these rights by institutions or people to whom one would look for some kind of leadership. I cite this as merely one instance, simply to show that in the broad course of history Canada is by no means Simon pure. We cannot, therefore, look at Watergate in the United States and say that nothing like that could happen here.
The speaker who preceded me said that the present provisions in the laws of Canada would make a Watergate a clear possibility here. I would like to say that this bill, which in part does deal in a positive way with the invasion of privacy, would still leave the possibility open to the Solicitor General of Canada to initiate the same kind of situation in Canada, and so long as that kind of legal possibility remains I do not think the bill merits support.
Mr. Terry O Connor (Halton): Mr. Speaker, the re-introduction before this House of legislation governing electronic surveillance has been welcomed by virtually all commentators. I join in this general commendation, but would add the comment that such action is long overdue. The subject has received lengthy scrutiny in previous parliaments. At least three previous Justice and Legal Affairs Committees have heard evidence and considered the matter of wiretap legislation, as it is generally called. It would be redundant to examine fully all of the arguments for and against such legislation at this time, nor is it necessary at this stage to examine in depth all of the particulars of Bill C-176. But I do wish to make a few comments of a general nature on the bill before the House.
The nefarious practice of the invasion of the personal privacy of the individual, without his knowledge or consent and without the authority of law, is surely an area which should be the subject of the most stringent government legislation. Yet as the law now stands such practice is not illegal, is not contrary to the Criminal Code and is not, per se, even the subject of civil action in eight of the provinces of Canada. These facts are sometimes not recognized or not understood by some of those who view the introduction of such legislation only in its permissive aspects, that is, as the allowing of the electronic surveillance of private conversations by police agencies.
This bill should be looked upon, as it definitely is, as a codification of something which most people take for granted as a fundamental human right, that of protection of the personal privacy of the individual and his freedom from interference with his personal conversations, his
Protection of Privacy
comings and goings, and his private affairs. Perhaps because of the inherently despicable nature of wiretapping, of bugging and the use of electronic recording equipment to learn of private communications, the general public seems to assume that these practices are illegal. But not so, Mr. Speaker. Thus, legislation in this field is welcomed wholeheartedly. One can only wonder why it took the government so long finally to put together Bill C-6 of the last parliament and now Bill C-176, the latter being substantially the same as the former.
In proposing rules and regulations of this type, however, the government must resolve the age-old and perhaps insoluble conundrum which faces the law when dealing with matters of this nature, the conflict which results when the interests of the individual are pitted in opposition to the interests of society as a whole. The extent and limitations of each, and the degree to which a contemporary society feels the already hazy line between the two should shift one way or the other, is a dilemma which has been faced by lawmakers in free countries over the centuries. A variation of this question is seen presently, especially in the United States, in the debate being waged over the freedom of the press to report, and thus the public to be informed, when such right may conflict with the right of the individual to receive a fair and equitable trial under the law. Thus, this bill must determine clearly for the courts the extent to which, and under what conditions, the public, through its authorized agencies may encroach upon the privacy of the individual.
It cannot be said that one right is paramount over the other, although we must start from the premise that the right of the individual to privacy is a fundamental human freedom which cannot be subrogated arbitrarily. But, to the extent that conflicting interests are diametrically opposed, there must be some compromise. The areas where clearly each is paramount must be spelled out and the hitherto hazy no man's land must be clearly defined. This bill, as did its predecessor, has attempted to achieve this goal in several commendable ways. First, it establishes as a criminal offence punishable by up to five years imprisonment, the use of electronic devices to intercept private communications without the consent of those involved. This operative section obviously refers to the wiretapping of telephone calls, the most common type of interception, but is broad enough to include the use of hidden microphones, long distance microphones and hidden recording devices. To these extents, it establishes as part of our codified law, the right of an individual to privacy.
Second, the bill permits exceptions to the general rule in the case of police and other security agencies, provided authority has been obtained to do so in accordance with the Criminal Code. The significant feature of this provision is the fact that the onus is clearly on those who wish to except themselves from criminal sanction, to establish the necessity to resort to such methods of collecting evidence. The application for the authority is made to a judge and must be signed by the Attorney-General of the province or his personally delegated agent. This requirement of political approval, which was not contained in the former Bill C-6, is an attempt to meet the objections of a

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
number of groups and individuals who have commented on the old bill. Groups with as traditionally disparate points of view as the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, however, managed to agree on this point.
The CACP brief to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs stated:
The responsibility for the issuance of permits or warrants must rest with the elected representatives and not with the judiciary ...
The civil liberties brief submitted to the committee on this point concludes:
We submit that the initiative for wire tapping application should reside with a political authority such as the Attorney General...
As I said, Mr. Speaker, the Bill C-176 has been changed apparently to achieve this effect. In fact, under the bill, electronic surveillance authorization would require the consent of the Attorney General or his agent and a judge. In the tried and true tradition of Liberal governments, they have tried to satisfy everyone and be all things to all men. But in the process they have compromised themselves into an error-one of the few in this legislation.
The whole question of the invasion of the sacredness of individual privacy is extremely delicate in nature. Its use or non-use should be determined by someone who is immediately accountable to the people-in other words only the Attorney General of a province or the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Allmand). A judge and our judicial system together with all of its built-in safeguards for those accused of crime, will eventually become involved in the process when examining the evidence adduced as a result of the wiretap. But the initial infringement of the state into the individual's private communications is a decision of the highest political order. It should, therefore, be made only by a politician, after which it may be the subject of public scrutiny and criticism in the public forum of a legislature or parliament. It follows, further, from this argument that the Attorney General should net be permitted to delegate this authority or if he is to be permitted to do so, such delegation should be to a severely limited number of individuals only and who would be known to the public either by name or position.
The bill in its present forms permits the delegation of this function, which should be properly that of an Attorney General, to as many agents as he so chooses. Presumably these could include every Crown Attorney, justice of the peace, or even chief of police in the province of the Attorney-General if he so wished. Clearly, there must be some statutory restraint in this area, either by the limitation of the function of granting such permission to the Attorney-General only or at least a limitation of the number of agents he may appoint, to a publicly known few. Surely, it is not anticipated that the use of such investigatory methods will be so broad as to unduly take up the time of a provincial Attorney General in examining the signing consents to proceed. And surely there can be few pursuits of greater importance to an Attorney General than the determination of such fundamental questions as the rights of the individual to prevent the indiscriminate delegation of this most important and onerous responsibility as the bill now does is wrong and ought not to be part of the legislation.
Five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of taking steps under the appropriate programmes to designate Saint-Hyacinthe as a special area in order to provide for the economic expansion of Saint-Hyacinthe by means of incentives to its industries; to bring about substantial industrial growth; and, by means of financial aid, to construct community facilities such as water, sewers, roads, and schools.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my great honour to introduce this motion in the hope that its importance for the population of Saint-Hyacinthe will be apparent to all my colleagues and will obtain the necessary approval, thus breaking with the unfortunate tradition by which such motions are debated to death, or until the debaters are exhausted.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext: That is what will happen!

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note the words of the member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), who says: "That is what will happen!" It will be a sorry thing for the constituency of Saint-Hyacinthe if that does happen.
Mr. Speaker, I should like right away to say what should be the spirit of this debate. We should take steps to have the Saint-Hyacinthe region designated as a "Special area", so as to provide economic development, and give a considerable boost to the agricultural, manufacturing and industrial sectors; that, briefly, is the spirit behind my presentation of this motion.
Through the words of its Member of Parliament, the whole population, the whole Saint-Hyacinthe area is now asking the federal government, first to help it boost the industries that area already there, second to help it bring
May 7, 1973

new businesses to it, and lastly, to help it bring about improvements in its community services.
The citizens of the Saint-Hyacinthe economic "subarea" can ask for a special intervention by the federal government with legitimate pride, for they have first helped themselves.
In the opinion of economists, the manpower of my riding is, and rightly so, recognized as stable and reliable. The infrastructures are in place, all ready to receive and support expansion projects or any new development plan.
The mayors of municipalities, particularly Mayor Gre-goire Girard of Saint-Hyacinthe, most municipal councils, the secretary treasurers or clerks, the agencies honourably representing our workers, the Chamber of Commerce, the Industrial Development Board and its dedicated officers, and, finally, the local news media well rooted in the riding, such as CKBS, Le Nouveau Clairon and Le Courrier, or because this paper also serves our riding, La Voix de VEst, they all support us, they all stand behind me as far as the submission of this request is concerned, rather, I should say, they are before me, because they preceded me.
They and others believed in the potential of Saint-Hyacinthe and, as early as 1969-70, they fought with my deserving predecessor, the hon. Theogene Ricard, to secure justice for Saint-Hyacinthe. I am quite aware of the fact that the Saint-Hyacinthe file is already bulky and significant in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The former minister, now Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), will recall having received on April 20, 1970, an impressive delegation from Saint-Hyacinthe, led by the common front of that have-not area. The minister, although he did not grant the request of the delegates, recognized that the situation was unfortunate for the Saint-Hyacinthe area, stating, and I quote:
The situation is abnormal and dangerous.
Mr. Speaker, three years after this April 1970 action of its common front, Saint-Hyacinthe is still in a bad way. Because of its designation as a "C" area, Saint-Hyacinthe offers little interest for the expansion of industry. Granby and Drummondville, closely related to Saint-Hyacinthe as to industrial stagnation, because of certain qualifications-so much the better for those towns and areas- have been designated as "B" areas. This, these two subareas, which are close neighbours are more attractive to industries wishing to locate south of Montreal.
On another plane, the decision taken by the minister in charge of housing on August 14, 1969, to bring an abrupt end to the urban renewal program has been dearly paid by the people of the Saint-Hyacinthe area in particular. Urban renewal studies had then cost the city of Saint-Hyacinthe $11,000, and the other levels of government $33,000. What is more, Mr. Speaker, the federal government's refusal at the time to allow the program to go ahead, would have caused at least a delay in the economic development of Saint-Hyacinthe and its surroundings. Building, business and, quite simply, all industry could have been boosted with investments.
Regional Economic Development
What lies ahead for Saint-Hyacinthe is even more disquieting. The study by the Quebec Planning and Development Bureau suggests that in the south of Montreal, in areas like Valleyfield and Saint-Hyacinthe, unemployment and stagnation have set in for a long time. The study carried out by the National Institute for Scientific Research even says, and I quote:
There will be very little increase in employment in Bagot, as the economy is predominantly agricultural. Unless there is some exchange with neighbouring counties, or some definitive migration, this part of the federal county of Saint-Hyacinthe will have a high rate of unemployment.
In the (provincial) counties of Saint-Hyacinthe and Rouville, the available manpower will seek work elsewhere because of the slow growth of employment.
In a word, the outlook seems favourable only in the constituencies located to the south of Montreal, along the river, from Chauteauguay to Sorel, and in the areas around Granby and Drummondville.
However-as the minister knows very well-the urban area of Saint-Hyacinthe, to name but one, has at least as many advantages as Granby. Indeed, from 1966 to 1971, Granby, whose town councillors must here be commended for their dynamism, created at least three times as many new jobs as Saint-Hyacinthe and Valleyfield together.
All this brings us to wonder whether the distance from Montreal is a very valid criterion for a zone to be designated or not by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
At a time when it is about to renew its programs, it is fitting to call the Department of Regional Economic's attention to certain features.
First of all, considering Quebec as a whole, it is obvious that the province needs a master plan, and also close consultation with provincial and municipal authorities and with the main intermediary bodies concerned.
Considering the situation of Saint-Hyacinthe specifically the department should be made aware of the urgent need for more equitable administration of the master plan, particularly regarding neighbouring Granby and Drummondville and for greater autonomy in relation to Montreal itself.
That, Mr. Speaker, is why in my plea-and it is a plea- on behalf of the population of Saint-Hyacinthe, I should just like to point out a few reforms the department could consider implementing.
In the first place, consideration should be given to a contingency for regional stabilisation fund. This would be an instrument for assistance through public investments to industrial towns at times of economic crisis or when industrial economy is functioning normally, to towns dealing mainly in services.
Government interventions should be concentrated in locations which have better opportunities, due to their own facilities, to resist the Montreal attraction, especially Saint-Hyacinthe, to name one among others.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that Montreal should become an economic monstrosity or any such thing. Not at all. It would be advisable, for example, to consider the
3486

May 7, 1973
Regional Economic Development possible substitution of regional industrial parks for municipal industrial parks. We should for example consider industrial diversification which must also become a more inportant criterion of regional development.
From another point of view, Mr. Speaker, the partly agricultural vocation of Saint-Hyacinthe must hold the attention of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. We must consider the possibility of producing beef in the Montreal area and as again suggested by the National Institute for Scientific Research the other Quebec farming districts would recover most of the manufacturing milk production from the Montreal area. And above all, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, when it does consider the case of Saint-Hyacinthe in particular, will have to think about the definite establishment of a food farming industry, for sure, which will eventually create new jobs at home.
And before concluding this much too succinct analysis, I would like, still in the perspective of the economic development of Saint-Hyacinthe, to remind the government ministers about these urgent requirements: first, an urgent requirement for an expansion of the veterinary medicine school in Saint-Hyacinthe; second, an urgent requirement for a federal legislation concerning the production of sugar beets in order to enable farmers of my riding, in particular, as well as the Saint-Hilaire refinery, to enjoy more stable and considerable incomes; third, as requested by the Chamber of Commerce of Saint-Hyacinthe and the municipality of Beloeil, among others, to proceed with the integral of partial development of a master plan for an express transport system linking Montreal, Beloeil, Saint-Hyacinthe and the other municipalities involved.
Mr. Speaker, I become here only the spokesman for the people of the Saint-Hyacinthe area to ask, in closing, to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion that, in the decisions he will soon render in conjunction with the Quebec provincial government, Saint-Hyacinthe be considered very seriously as a "special area".
There are nonetheless some factors that are obvious. The rate of unemployment which last June was 13.2 per cent; the fact that the regional industries are unable to absorb the ever growing number of young people who complete their education and want to join the labour force; the fact that the district of Saint-Hyacinthe is classed as zone "C" by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which places it in a lower position than the neighbouring cities of Granby and Drummondville, which, in fact, are not much farther from Montreal than Saint-Hyacinthe. All these, and many others that I will be glad to give to the minister by hand, plead in favour of Saint-Hyacinthe.
Mr. Speaker, I would be grateful if this plea were not without results. I want to continue increasing the contacts I have already established with the minister himself and with the officials of the department, in order to multiply industries in the Saint-Hyacinthe constituency, to make maximum use of resources available at the federal level and, finally, to reach the point where this worthy cause of the Saint-Hyacinthe population will be heard, accepted

and fostered by the officers of the department, not only for the benefit of the people of Saint-Hyacinthe but for the benefit of all our fellow citizens.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) for the brilliant plea he has just made to have his area designated as a special area. It is my humble opinion that the department is now looking for reasons which could warrant the designation of areas in most of low growth areas in Canada.
In my first speech to this House I talked about my area. I note that what was pointed out a while ago by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe strangely ressembles what is happening in my riding of Sherbrooke; the unemployment figures are the same. During the last two and a half years, or even three, studies were made by university researchers as well as the Sherbrooke city council to have the department designate the Sherbrooke area and, on a larger scale, the Eastern Townships as a special area.
We know quite well that our area-here I am thinking mainly of the Sherbrooke area-is in great need of secondary industries. As early as 1954 we developed a tertiary sector which, in my humble opinion, stands second to none in other big Quebec cities. The University of Sherbrooke as well as the University Medical Centre have contributed for a large part to the development of our area.
But if we consider what has been done in the field of processing industries we realize that in the past 10 years, if we figure out the number of industries which settled in the area and the number of those which left, we are minus one. Therefore, our area as well as that of Saint-Hyacinthe have been disfavoured in that respect in comparison to other areas of the country.
In my humble opinion-and I hope the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe will forgive me-the Eastern Townships and more particularly the area of Sherbrooke which is the queen of the Eastern Townships is in the great need of industries and its designation as special area would help enormously in setting up an infrastructure which would allow secondary industries which we lack to settle there.
The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe has indicated a few minutes ago that almost 13 per cent of the population was unemployed in his region. We have the same figure for the Sherbrooke region. However, we have a problem in our region which perhaps is not found in that of Saint-Hyacinthe since it is close to the metropolis of Canada, and it has benefitted for many years from some developments on the outskirts of Montreal; Saint-Hyacinthe has even been described as being or becoming a bedroom town, and I agree with the member for Saint-Hyacinthe when he says that development is much slower when such things happen.
Mr. Speaker, I will support such a motion provided the Eastern Townships be designated at the same time, that is to say that slow growing regions include-and that is the responsibility of the department-all developing regions- and let us put these words between quotation marks-"of Quebec and the east of our country" as well as other regions which have been disadvantaged in many respect because of big poles of growth.
May 7, 1973

Mr. Speaker, while I agree with the proposal of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, I think that representations now being made by the department to the government of the province of Quebec will have some results, aware as I am that a "special area" cannot be designated without the approval of provinces, and that during the next few weeks, the premier of Quebec as well as the federal Minister of Regional Expansion (Mr. Jamieson)-

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext: -as well as the parliamentary secretary!

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext: -and the parliamentary secretary will hold discussions to gain an insight into what can be done about slow growing regions in the province of Quebec. I hope that at that time, not only the city of Saint-Hyacinthe but that of Sherbrooke as well will be considered, since we have been making representations for three years already to the minister so that our region be taken into account. I am not the only one to say so; studies made recently by the Quebec Planning and Development Bureau show that the Eastern Townships are economically ill, need a lot of economic assistance as well as an input of capital. This could be done by designating our region as a "special area".

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I express sympathy with the two hon. members who are seeking to have their particular areas designated under the auspices of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. If this debate were to continue for two or three days, I am sure every Member of Parliament from every comer of the country would like to see his area designated. This does not speak well for the last one hundred years of economic development in Canada, though it does speak well for members who present a case for their areas.
I would point out to the hon. members who have spoken that a year or two ago the government proposed to deal with the question of the designation of areas under the DREE program. There has been, since then, a suspension of that revision process. Certainly, the two cases presented by the preceding speakers ought to be reviewed by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson). I am not well acquainted with those areas, but undoubtedly some day I shall enjoy visiting them. I do say that the question of the revision of designated areas should be dealt with by the minister as soon as possible.
There are certainly questions which need to be asked in terms of designation as they relate to unemployment, to the migration of population from rural areas to urban areas and the continuation of that migration in many parts of the country. If you look at my home province of Saskatchewan you will find that the designated area might well be expanded across most of the north. There are only two areas picked out for designation, in a sense; one in Meadow Lake and one east of Saskatoon. They happen to cover the two seats which were held by two Liberals in that province, but I will not go into that.
The question of regional expansion is one with a far more expansive perspective than merely where lines were
Regional Economic Development
drawn in terms of incentive grants. There is a real need for a review and revaluation of those very grants to determine how effective they have been in regional development. If you study the statistics related to poverty in Canada, if you studies the statistics related to development in areas which have been economically deprived in this country, you will find, Mr. Speaker, that in the last four years in the operation of regional development there has been no substantial change in the situation in those regions of Canada which need development, that is to say, regions which lie outside the Ontario golden horseshoe.
We need far more concrete answers about the operation of this program than we have been getting from the minister so far in the committee on regional development. We have had no information about the evaluation of the program which supposedly has been taking place in the last three years. There has been no indication of when those studies are to take place. The minister stated in his forty-page statement to the committee when the committee was dealing with the department that there would be a reevaluation, a redefinition of the type of grants given, a decentralization of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. He stated that the question of equity would be dealt with.
I need only refer to the Ottawa Citizen of April 5 of this year in which the minister is reported as saying that DREE might take back shares in aided firms. There has been no answer whatsoever from the minister to these questions as they relate to economic expansion. I hope that when the committee begins again tomorrow we shall get assurances as to an evaluation of this program up until this point in time. This is needed in order to improve it and develop it for the future. An assessment should be made showing how many of these grants have in fact been give-aways. The minister stated that 70 per cent of the grants made so far were needed in order to create jobs. This simply means that 30 per cent was, in a sense, not needed and that the jobs would have been created anyway. This could represent a loss or a waste in a sense to the Canadian taxpayer of some $100 million. I am sure the new minister is sincere. He comes from a region which itself needs assistance. He has to give the committee some concrete evidence on which to work, a concrete proposal to convince us there is to be some redirection of this department which has come under such severe criticism in the last few years.
We have heard a great deal in answer to questions in the House and in committee to the effect that certain things will be done or will be considered, but we have not received from this department one concrete proposal, other than in respect of decentralization, for real change in the future. I hope the committee will deal with the criteria to be used in the designation of areas, as well as with the question of whether the federal government should take action in respect of equity in the use of Canadian tax dollars in spite of the pleas of multinational corporations. This matter is particularly important in respect of publicly-owned corporations in all parts of the country.
The committee should also deal directly with the freight rate structure as it affects regional development. The
3488

May 7, 1973
Regional Economic Development Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) was previously minister of transport and knows the effect of the freight rate structure on my area of the country, on northern Ontario and the Maritimes. Prominent people have told me that when it comes to developing industry in southern Saskatchewan such as distilling and using products from the area, the fundamental obstacle is not lack of incentives or grants for regional development but freight rates on the finished product. If policies of regional development are to work they must take into account questions such as transportation.
I could make a long speech about the effectiveness of DREE grants, but I would sum up by saying that in many instances, although not all, these grants represent nothing more than corporate write-offs. I hope the committee will in the coming weeks inquire into the equity of our transportation policy and will obtain concrete proposals from the minister and his assistants for the development of a truly regional development program.
During our discussions on designation of areas I hope the matter of unemployment will be seriously taken into account. In addition, I hope the question of the emigration of regional population will be taken into account, Hon. members from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, as well as members from the Prairies, know it is not easy to assess the unemployment situation in these areas because of the movement of population to industrial centres resulting from lack of employment in regional areas. This situation must also be considered.
Designation should not be based on only one economic year. A good example of this is found in the western regions where because of grain sales by the Canadian Wheat Board the economy of one year may be relatively high yet within less than a year it can take a severe drop. One year of adverse weather conditions can result in substantial economic change in some areas. When it comes to designation, consideration should be given to the instability of certain economies within Canada.
In conclusion, I wish the hon. member well in his attempt to obtain for his area recognition under DREE. I hope that in the weeks before the summer recess we will receive concrete proposals from the minister. If we believe these proposals represent a move in the right direction, I can promise the House that we will not be as critical as in the past; we will openly welcome any substantial changes in this direction.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was indeed pleased to hear the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) indicate that he will not be as critical in the future.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext: Provided you do something.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF DESIGNATING ST. HYACINTHE AS A SPECIAL AREA
speechtext:
I was pleased that the hon. member for Assiniboia, who is one of our more active members on the committee on regional economic expansion, participated effectively in this debate. However, I hope his initial criticism, probably unjustified, will not mislead him in future discussions to frustrate the studies being conducted by that committee. I am sure he recognizes that the program

being reviewed by the committee, pursuant to the declaration of the minister, was initiated in 1969 and that some time must be taken in order to ascertain its effects. I agree that there will have to be some amelioration of the program.
I come from an area similar to that of the hon. member for Assiniboia and I hope that in the future we will be able to work together to adopt the best measures for our respective regions. I am pleased, in view of the initial criticism of the hon. member for Assiniboia, to note how readily the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) agreed on the effectiveness of DREE as put into effect by the government. As a result of his ability to argue and plead his case with sincerity, we are convinced that he really believes this program is of great economic benefit.
However, I was somewhat apprehensive about the intentions of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) since his motion was placed on the order paper on January 12, 1973, while he was asked to introduce it on three occasions, namely on February 5, on February 19 and on March 19. I want to oppose the motion of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, because I believe that the available funds to encourage economic expansion are limited and that they should be affected to areas which should be able to ensure in the future a development which is likely to favour all the other areas in Canada.
Moreover, I would simply like to say that the Saint-Hyacinthe area has the same advantages as the Montreal area. In fact, as of December 31, 1972, the Department had offered ten grants which were accepted by applicants in Saint-Hyacinthe. The amounts involved totaled $618,000 and was to create 281 direct jobs. 16 grants offered and accepted, for a total amount of $763,591 and 425 direct jobs having been created.

And I want precisely to talk about that subject because the whole of the Montreal area is considered as one economic region. And again on the subject of my own area, I will say that it is just like any area in Northern Quebec. Let me quote from the report the minister filed with the committee when he appeared for the first time. This is what it said:
In a large area of the province, encompassing the bulk of provincial territory and almost 800,000 people, economic performance has been more like that of Manitoba or New Brunswick than that of the rest of Ontario. Northern Ontario has experienced a growth rate in population of less than one per cent per year throughout the decade of the 1960's, slightly below the average for the Atlantic region. It tends to be characterized by a dual economy comprising urban centres such as Thunder Bay, Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury, North Bay and Timmins, where incomes are at or above national averages, and rural and remote areas and resource towns, where incomes tend to be substantially below the Canadian average and where economic growth depends almost entirely upon primary resource production.
And this area is not designated as a special area, as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe would like for his own area.

I deeply sympathize with those people who were so badly tried. However, his is a metropolitan region, and he has access to the provincial government, and he knows very well that the program he wishes to see implemented requires a preliminary agreement between the provincial and the federal governments. True enough, he knows several of the members sitting in the Quebec national assembly and he could certainly approach them and ask for assistance.
Obviously, the motion before us requires to be very seriously considered and I think that all those who took part in the debate have done so.
Mr. Speaker, I only want to say, as every one speaks about his own church belfry, that mine needs to be repainted and that the sound of the bell is not as clear as it should be. In fact, in my area as in most other areas of the country there is a need, not only for temporary stimulants but for one that will favour providing a substructure enabling the manufacturing industry to settle down permanently.
As the Minister of Regional Economic Development has very ably indicated, Northern Ontario has to be developed in order to provide for the development of the far-north-

Mr. Speaker, I have been very happy to take this opportunity once again to bring not only my riding and its problems but also all the surrounding regions to the attention of the whole country.
Let's come back to the riding of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe. At the outset of discussions held in 1969 and 1970 with the Quebec government concerning the designation of special areas in the province, they deemed advisable not to concentrate efforts on the Montreal region, because the employment situation in Montreal and the neighbouring areas had not yet deteriorated enough to warrant its designation under one of the departmental programs. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to private members' hour I was pointing out what in my opinion is the one major flaw in this bill, that is, the provision to refer an application for authorization to wiretap to a combination of both a judge and the attorney general of a province. I feel this requirement as set out in the bill is the result of an attempted compromise by the government to satisfy those proponents of authorization being granted by a judge and at the same time to satisfy those proponents of authorization being granted by an attorney general.
In its attempt to compromise, the government has tried to spread the responsibility for making decision. It is neither that alone of the attorney general, his agent or a judge, but of both or perhaps all of them. This approach, in my opinion, is a worse alternative than leaving the decision solely to a judge. At least then one person alone is responsible for the decision taken. The bill now invites a buck-passing exercise with perhaps no one being accountable for a foolish or harmful use of the authority.
If we recognize that the individual's right to privacy can only be interfered with in the event of public necessity
May 7, 1973

where harm to the public or members of it will possibly follow without its use, then someone must be directly responsible for ensuring that individual rights are protected. The buck must stop somewhere. In my opinion it should be with the Attorney General or Solicitor General alone.
The bill quite properly limits the duration of the use of individual instances of electronic surveillance, requires periodic public accounting of the use of such electronic devices and allows the emergency use of the right to intercept a communication where circumstances do not permit a formal application to be made. There is provision for the awarding of damages to a person aggrieved by one convicted of employing electronics surveillance equipment contrary to the bill, and this again is commendable.
The thrust of the bill, with which I agree, is to make an offence the odious practice of intercepting private conversations except where such practices are necessary in the combating of crime, and only then after close scrutiny and authorization by a properly designated and responsible person. The increasing sophistication of criminal activities and organized, syndicated crime, all equipped with mechanical and electronic equipment, demands that police agencies be allowed the use of equally effective equipment. If the rights of the individual can be safeguarded by judicious and scrutinized use of such equipment, then such use should be a permitted exception to the general prohibition. But for the reasons I have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is necessary that the person responsible for the decision to allow the use of such investigatory methods must be the Attorney General or the Solicitor General of Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, much of what has been said by my colleagues in this debate so far has gone to the merits or demerits of the bill and has dealt with some of the particular facts and circumstances of the proposals. I think the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), the hon. member for Halton (Mr. O'Connor) and the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) have dealt exceptionally well with the detail of the bill and I associate myself to a considerable extent with what they have said. I do want to point out that in our examination of this bill we must not forget that it does in fact constitute an extension of the right of the state to secure from people involuntary information or involuntary statements.
I know that the minister said, and I accept his statement, that there is a limitation on the extent to which information derived from electronic surveillance and so-called bugging can be taken. Nevertheless, by this bill there is an extension of the right of government, the right of the state to secure information which in the past it might have had the legal right but certainly it did not have the moral right to obtain.
In my view, in the long run, particularly after the circumstances which we have seen displayed in recent days in other parts of the world, there is a growing body of public opinion opposed to invasion of privacy by means which are unknown to the people whose statements are being obtained in that way. All through the centuries states have attempted to secure facts and information by involuntary means. Any historical examination of this
Protection of Privacy
phenomenon will go back to the days of the Inquisition. I do not limit only to the Inquisition but I use the Inquisition as an example, as an historical incident best known to people in the modern day who have read about it. Many methods have been used in an attempt to secure information-by force and by torture both mental and physical. Over the years a repugnance has grown up to this form of acquiring facts and information even in the course of securing information for the prosecution of criminal offences and protecting society.
There has been this conflict. You need to protect society, it is true, but you need to do it by means which are acceptable, not repugnant, to the individual. You may sometimes gain by purporting to guard the state but you may lose infinitely more through the means of securing that information if you brutalize society and the individuals engaged in obtaining it. Before and during the last war we saw evidence of this in the totalitarian states. There are totalitarian states today, of course. I am not going to go into detail about them, but it is common knowledge that they are engaged in securing information not only by electronic surveillance but by other means as well.
This constant struggle has not been won nor, I suppose, will it ever be won because of the very nature of government and the innate character of any kind of government. I confess quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, that if I were a member of a government I would not trust such methods without taking steps to ensure that the strongest possible protection was taken through checks and balances and countervailing forces. What we have here is simply an extension of that principle. When this debate is over, it is true that within the four corners of the bill will be found certain restrictions upon the extent to which the state can go to secure information, without the knowledge of the people involved, by means of electronic and mechanical devices of surveillance. In the result, we will have codified a right of government. By this bill we are saying, in effect, that government has a right to certain types of information without the knowledge, suspicion or consent of the people involved, the right to secure information and statements from them by means of such devices.
I would like this bill to have contained a preamble stating that it is contrary to the rights of the people of this land that there be any electronic surveillance, bugging of any kind except subject to certain exceptions; in other words, an extension of the Bill of Rights. The bill should start on the basis that it is wrong, it is improper, it is not the right of government to secure information by these means unless subject to certain rules. We do not have that; we have a recognition by this bill, not only by implication but by expressed statement that it is right, it is proper and it is legal. I am concerned about this question even though that statement is coupled with other language which restricts the right.
I suggest to the minister that he include a preamble-it might be possible to put it in the Bill of Rights or other legislation-to the effect that the innate principle of securing involuntary statements through electronic surveillance is wrong to start with and can be approved only on certain conditions, some of which would be contained in the bill. As it is now, we have a codification and an

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
admission. By this legislation this House is saying that in fact we approve the right to do it under certain circumstances. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that while we may give very limited blessing to this proposition and may comfort ourselves by saying we have so hedged it with restrictions that it can be done only under certain circumstances, the whole history of parliamentary legislation is that once entry is made, slowly and inexorably the practice grows.
Some of my colleagues may remember when the original income tax bill was passed. 1 was not here at that time nor, I believe, was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I think it was called the war income tax act and was referred to as temporary, as an act for the purpose of securing certain funds to carry on the war. That was during the First World War, and the people who passed that legislation were probably beguiled by statements of the government of the day, which I believe was a government of a persuasion which should have known better. But at least it was a unionist government. It said that the legislation was temporary and would be withdrawn as soon as the war was over. If Members of Parliament of that day had seen the miscalled tax reform legislation recently introduced in this House, I think they would have given it a terrible time; those people who observe cemeteries might have noticed that the ground was rather disturbed where some of these legislators now are.
When this legislation has been in effect for some time, Mr. Speaker, I wager that people will be coming to governments of the future pleading special cases which will suggest that the principle of the bill should be extended. I make the prediction, confident that it is correct, that in ten or fifteen years from this small beginning of a legislative approval the right to electronic surveillance with be substantially extended. That is why I would feel much more comfortable with the ultimate passage of this legislation if it were preceded by a preamble which said that the principle, to start with, was wrong and only under certain circumstances could it be allowed.
I leave that part of the bill and the debate, Mr. Speaker, because I want now to deal with another aspect which was referred to by my hon. friend from Fundy-Royal. He said that in dealing with this matter the government should deal with a companion question of the right of freedom of information. These are Siamese twins; they are inextricably bound together and cannot be dissociated one from the other. The government secures all kinds of information, not only that given on income tax forms but data on various questionnaires and documents sent out by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and by Statistics Canada. Ask any small businessman. There is an undue, continuing encroachment upon the rights of individual citizens of this country who wish to retain information of a private nature. Indeed, today there is little information that an individual cannot be compelled to give to some appropriate authority of government, particularly the federal government. This applies also to provincial governments and to the governments of some cities.
If one were to make a detailed, itemized list of all legislation passed by parliament for compelling an

individual to provide information to governments, one would be astounded at the extent of legislation which compels one to divulge facts. This may be necessary; I do not know. In any event, the government comes into possession of a tremendous amount of information. If this bill passes, it is obvious that the government could come into possession of a great deal more information. What, then, is the responsibility of government in the use of that information?
There is a growing feeling on the part of governments all over the world, which includes this government and the government of the United States, that the executive branch of government stands in some rare, exclusive and esoteric position vis-a-vis the rest of the people of the country. This administration is gathering facts and information and feels it has no responsibility to make known the facts which it has obtained. I consider that to be a dangerous and pernicious doctrine, particularly as it is held by a government which is now seeking this means of compelling further facts and information to be divulged involuntarily.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal referred to a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) before he assumed his onerous responsibilities. At that time he was much more liberal in his views and spoke as a small "1" liberal about social and legal problems in this country. He was not the only one who held that view and made statements of that kind. While luxuriating in the freedom of not being the prime minister of this country and being free to say what he thought, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), writing in the Montreal periodical Cite Libre, took a strong stand on the need of the public for true and complete information. Although dealing with Quebec politics, he made a statement that basically referred to any democratic government. On that occasion he said:
Democratic progress requires the ready availability of true and complete information. In this way, the people can objectively evaluate their government's policies.
To act otherwise is to give way to despotic secrecy.
Those are the words of the leader of the government which we face every Monday and Wednesday in our attempt to obtain answers to written questions and to secure documents. Many questions are asked. I would be the first to admit, and I see the parliamentary secretary pricking up his ears, that without doubt many questions are asked which should not be asked.

failed to live up to what the Prime Minister said before he became prime minister, before he even undertook his responsibilities as a member of this House. Many people hold the same opinion. Former United States president James Madison once said:
A popular government without popular information or the means of acquiring it, is but a prologue to a farce or a tragedy or perhaps both.
In speaking of the government he was referring to the legislature. Any country in which the legislature, the people and the press are inadequately informed of what the government is doing or what it plans is not a good country, because if information is withheld from parliament there is no forum wherein the affairs of the nation can be debated adequately and properly.
That this is so has been demonstrated by what has happened in the last few weeks in the United States. I do not intend to become involved in what is happening there. The trouble is not so much what some individuals are alleged to have done in their electronic surveillances and in the securing of facts; it is that they are alleged to have taken extravagant and unusual steps to withhold that knowledge from the people. That is the trouble they are in today and that is the reason for their difficulty. The question at issue involves not only what was done, juvenile, stupid and silly though it was; it also involves the failure of certain people to impart frankly and honestly the facts to the people. The attitude of that government is much the same as the attitude held by members of this government. It is alleged that that administration feels that certain facts and information which may be too esoteric, too embarrassing, too difficult or too damaging must not and need not be disclosed.
Before this House complies with the request of the government to give the government or its emanations the right to secure further information, the minister some time before third reading, possibly in committee, should say that the government will take a serious look at the idea of codifying the rights of parliament, of the people and of the press to secure facts and information from the government.

I have proposed a bill dealing with this area. I do not for one moment suggest it is the final answer. To be honest, I have some doubts myself about parts of my proposal. This is the third time I have mentioned this bill in the House, which in one form or another has been before the House for about three years. I call it the right to information act. The term "public business" is defined in the bill. It contains a simple statement about the rights of Canadians. I suggest there should be a statement in this bill about the rights of Canadians to be free from electronic surveillance except under certain conditions. The rights in my bill are as follows:
Any Canadian, or any person not being a Canadian who resides in Canada, may apply to the government for a record made in the course of public business and the government shall, within a reasonable time thereafter, provide a copy of such record to any person who so applies or make such record available for inspection by him.
Protection of Privacy
There are certain exceptions; I admit that. In addition, I propose that if the government cannot bring itself within the four corners of those exceptions there is the right of the citizen to go to court in order to have the issue settled. If the court makes a declaration, there is then a mandatory duty upon the government, department or Crown corporation involved to furnish that information or face the penalty of a jail sentence. I do not think you would have to use the penalty provision very often, probably only once or twice.
The salutary effect of legislation of that kind becoming part of the law of this land would, in my opinion, have a very useful effect on a government which, because it is the government, is secretive to begin with and, because it is a Liberal government, is even more secretive than most governments. I suggest that this is not very far from the subject matter we are debating. The members of the standing committee to which this bill will be referred will be free to secure a statement from the government and the minister at that time. The former minister of justice, now Minister of Finance, made it quite plain; he said in the simplest and clearest language that it is essential that there be a legislative proposal of this kind. The time has long passed for this country to have on the statute books legislation which gives that right to the ordinary citizen of Canada.

speechtext:
If hon. friends to my left, and this party get together there will not only be the moral strength but the numerical strength of our conviction which will have a very strong effect on my friends opposite.
While coming back here the other day I was listening to the news. What struck me was not so much the Watergate case in the United States but the case of the Pentagon papers, the prosecution of two men. One does not need to

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
agree with them ideologically, politically or otherwise. It has now been pretty well established that the documents they took had in large part been published beforehand. Expert witnesses called at the trial of these two men testified beyond any question that the documents which they took and caused to be published were not secret documents in the sense they had any value or endangered in any way the prosecution of United States' participation in Indo-China. Most extraordinarily, we find that people high in the government and security agencies in the government were involved in burglary attempts and attempts to obscure information about these two defendants in order to try to favourably impress the judge and jury and forward the prosecution's case. These are the kinds of dangers we face in the matter we are dealing with today. We only see that part of the iceberg above the surface of the water.
This is an admirable opportunity for all members of the House to look at the whole problem in a non-partisan and objective way. The standing committee which will consider this bill is an excellent committee. I hope the committee will have the courage to be objective. It would be well advised to come back with very strong recommendations which the government would have to accept.
