Mr. Speaker, as a new member of this House I am surprised to learn that this is the third time this bill, in substance, has been before parliament. I understand that it has been dealt with extensively on three other occasions by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Having had that much time in committee and in this House, I find it incredible that the extensive rights to wiretap under the Official Secrets Act have not been removed from the bill.
I was impressed with the approach taken by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) in dealing with this subject as a matter of a bill of rights or a matter of being positive, rather than negative, in guaranteeing one's right to privacy. This is a most useful approach that could be taken.
It is also interesting to note there have been at least four private members' bills dealing directly with this subject; one from the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Mather), one from the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), one from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) before he held that post, and one from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). That persuades me there is some merit indeed in private members' bills. I am convinced this subject would probably not be before the House now without the pressure that has been put on the government by private members both now and in the past.
There is no doubt that severe regulation must come into the law with regard to the continuing flagrant abuse of privacy by electronic devices. This bill, which has many weaknesses, is still long overdue. I intend, as I believe the majority of the members of the New Democratic Party intend, to vote for this bill in principle and have it referred to committee. However, I must say we are most unhappy with many provisions in the bill. In fact, this is

just a little better than nothing. I would characterize this as still being basically Big Brother legislation.
We have to look upon this bill as only the beginning of a concerted attack upon violations of the right of privacy- violations by big business, by the large technocracy which is developing around us, by government itself. In the last 30 years the pendulum has been swinging away from individual privacy. It cannot swing back unless there is government help, governmental intervention.
I was most impressed by the position taken by the hon. member for Peace River. I was impressed by his argument that we should look at this question from the positive point of view and bring in a bill which would guarantee privacy, rather than the kind of bill we are now considering. The bill before us fails to deal with many areas of privacy violation. For example, we are still faced with flagrant abuses by credit reporting agencies affecting the rights of citizens across the country. What is needed is a bill to require the disclosure by all credit agencies of the files they keep on individuals.
We need a bill which gives to individual citizens the right to take action against such agencies when the information they possess is inaccurate. In addition, we need legislation giving the private citizen the right to clear his record, in the same way as a person convicted of criminal offences has a right to clear his criminal record. There may be items in a man's financial past which hurt his credit indefinitely. There should be some provision here to protect him from the disclosure of information by these agencies which could cause him serious harm.
We need legislation which would allow a citizen to challenge in the courts the release of private data about himself without his consent. I think, too, we need a bill of rights for employees so that employers are prevented from invading the personal lives of employees and interfering with their right to privacy. We do not need big corporations whose employees are expected to go to the company church, the company picnic, and so on. It seems to me that here, too, a right of independence and privacy is involved.
Last, but not least, we should consider protecting the right of privacy where the news media are concerned. I realize the news media should be entitled to get the news fairly when they can, but there are times when they step over the boundary, as it were, as when for example they take pictures of a mother grieving over a dead child. On many occasions in times of personal tragedy the news media impose upon a family that awesome thing, a television camera. In a way this, too, is an infringement of personal liberty and it is an area which those engaged in the media should themselves be considering very carefully.
To deal with the bill before us, there are still many points of weakness in it. First, it seems to me the bill gives authority for wiretapping to be carried out in all cases of indictable offences. I do not see why it should be allowed in all cases. I believe wiretapping should be limited to cases where the most serious offences are suspected. Are we to allow wire tapping for the purpose of catching marijuana smokers? Apparently, under this bill we could.
May 7, 1973______________COMMONS DEBATES_____________________3495
It seems to me that only the most serious crimes should be covered by the legislation and that these should be listed. Something in the order of those carrying at least a ten-year prison term should be considered.
There is no provision for the attorneys general of the provinces to be required to report to their legislatures in connection with the permits they have issued. This is a fundamental issue. If a political authority is to be allowed to issue permits for wiretapping, the final political authority should be the parliament. When an attorney general is not required to report back to parliament, a dictatorship situation arises.
The most severe weakness in the bill is one most speakers have already touched on. It involves the Official Secrets Act. In spite of the criticism which has so often been levelled at the government, this kind of legislation is foisted upon us. It is not good enough. Earlier I described the bill as Big Brother legislation. The clause I had in mind begins on page 21, and it provides:
The Solicitor General of Canada may issue a warrant authorizing the interception or seizure of any communication if he is satisfied by evidence on oath that. .. the purpose of such interception or seizure is related to the prevention or detection of espionage, sabotage-
These are the operative words which are so dangerous: -or any other subversive activity directed against Canada or detrimental to the security of Canada.
Under the provisions of this clause there is no responsibility to go to a judge. It is entirely an internal matter between the Solicitor General and the police force. This is most dangerous. We have no right to be smug about the Watergate case. Under our present laws, as other speakers have pointed out, there could be a Watergate, and I submit that we could just as easily see a Watergate under the bill before us, because of some solicitor general who was not able to draw the fine line between opposition and subversion. Exactly the same thing could occur here. This clause gives the Solicitor General the right to determine which organizations in the country can be placed under wiretap surveillance. It immediately brings to mind the question of political radicalism on campus, debating societies, and so on. We have already witnessed interference with political freedom on campus. I can see no protection for political freedom on campus in the terms of this bill. The RCMP has over and over again shown itself to be completely unsophisticated when it comes to determining what are political rights and what is sabotage.

They simply do not have the background or in many cases the education to understand it, and this can become a direct threat to academic and political freedom in this country. I want to deal briefly with one or two other clauses. We say that evidence obtained by wiretapping is inadmissible in court, yet evidence derived from wiretapping is admissible. Surely all we are doing here is encouraging illegal

wiretapping. The least that should be given is a voir dire in connection with such evidence, so that the judge can inquire as to the rights of the individuals concerned before that evidence is considered.
I hope these matters will be dealt with positively by the justice committee. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are certain elements in this legislation the thrust of which most of us agree with. I disagree with the previous speaker in that he is more inclined to put emphasis on serious offences. I agree with the legislation to the extent that it must relate to illegalities per se, whether the offence being investigated is major or minor, because interference with the right of the public to privacy must be protected and upheld. I think it is the function of parliament to maintain that privacy.
There are one or two technical matters to which I should like to refer. The first relates to an application for an ex parte motion. Any lawyer will know that ex parte motions are open to the public, and with a little contemplation this legislation could properly be altered to take care of that situation. It can be left to the committee to make some of these changes to which other speakers have alluded, but this is one which to date has perhaps been overlooked.
This bill calls for notice to be given an accused if this type of evidence, either by transcript, by tape or by whatever method is used, is to be used; but it does not say when. All the power of the state is being pitted against the accused. He must have some time to prepare his defence. Such a notice should not be handed to him at the time the evidence goes in, as that is hardly fair or in keeping with our concept of justice. Under the Ontario Medical Act, for example, in respect of medical evidence at least an accused is given seven days' notice. I think there should be some kind of time limitation, in respect of when notice is given, that such evidence is to be used against an accused. The accused should be given a copy of the transcript or the tape, as the case may be, in order that he will have fair warning and be in a position to prepare his defence.
I am worried about another aspect of this legislation. Although I am not an electronics expert, having watched television at times I am aware of how tapes can be doctored, and this bothers me. Tapes can be cut, spliced and put together, entirely changing the context of a conversation. This legislation in itself or through its regulations must have some safeguards to protect the accused and others if such evidence is to be used. I am not a cynic but, rather, a realist and having been in the courtroom day after day I know how some officials operate. Among the safeguards we have for accused, this legislation must

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
require some scientific proof that there has been no tampering with or doctoring of such tapes or transcripts.
Perhaps another minor point is the aspect of this legislation relating to the doctrine of possession. I have been greatly concerned about the word "knowing" in reference to the primary use. What is "primary"? How close is it to secondary or tertiary? This is a difficult question. The accused must show that possession was not for that primary use. From the accused's point of view, I think that part of the legislation must be further considered.
I am also bothered that peace officers would be authorized to have such equipment in their possession, but the legislation does not spell out that they must only be in possession when so authorized; it merely refers to possession as long as the peace officer is in the course of his employment. Most police officers are employed on a shift basis and may not have the authority to have such equipment in their possession, but if they do so this will not be an offence under the proposed change. Again, I do not want to appear cynical but we must realize that police officers are human and do have temptations. There must be safeguards to protect the general public, making sure that policemen do not abuse the privileges given them. This legislation must relate to the situation I have just outlined as well as to John Q. Public. It must also relate to policemen whether they are on duty or off duty, and those that do not have the authority must be treated in the same way as any other member of the public.
I am surprised by the degree of trust and equanimity we display in respect of those in charge of our communications in this country, telephone and telegraph. We accept them like we accept God and motherhood and believe they can do no wrong. Apparently they can interfere with communications because that is their business and they should know what is going on.
Our memories are very short indeed if we forget what was so well documented recently in respect of the state of IT&T and the way it operated during the last war. It owned 28 per cent of a German aircraft company which produced planes which shot down our aircraft, while at the same time producing communications equipment to protect our ships and planes. Apparently Colonel Ben did not worry about that situation. If we think our communications system is not tied up with IT&T, then we are naive to the point that we should not be sitting in this honourable chamber. All you need do is talk with employees of Northern Electric or Bell Telephone to find out what the connection is with IT&T.
In any event, that is the way IT&T operated during the last war. Its communications and espionage system was the best in the world. It initiated the first entente with Hitler right after he came to power. A committee of two from the United States made a visit in that regard, and Colonel Ben of IT&T was one of them. They were put in touch with the right people.
We must take a long, hard look at what I consider to be the very naive way in which we view communications conditions in this country. Parliament and the people have a right to be protected against the actions of such corporations. I frankly admit that I have no love for IT&T or for what it does. It sucks the blood of any person who comes along and tries to play both ends against the

middle. It forecast that Germany would win the war in 1941, yet in the middle of 1948 it claimed $27 million compensation for damage caused by our bombers to its aircraft plant. In any event, I believe we must take a more serious look at that aspect of this legislation.
In a philosophic way-others have referred to this-the section dealing with the Official Secrets Act actually codifies and allows the government to carry on what happened in the Watergate affair. I am sure hon. members across the way would suggest to me that this is all right if it is necessary in the public interest to keep them in government.

There is your answer, Mr. Speaker. The wording of the legislation is such that if the Solicitor General thinks it is necessary and in the public interest, the government can do what it wants to do. I do not know who the hon. member was who interjected just now, but I am glad he answered my question, because this is what can happen when a government thinks this legislation is necessary and good in the public interest. It can undertake any surveillance it wished: this legislation makes it possible. If John Stewart Mill were alive today, he would certainly roll in his grave.
I have become rather distrustful of politicians, because politicians too often want power, and power corrupts. Absolute power corrupts absolutely, and this is the temptation which this legislation places in the government's hands. I am afraid my mind wanders a bit, but while I was sitting here tonight I was concerned about the politician, what he actually does and what he stands for. A little limerick came to mind, which I would quote with your permission, Mr. Speaker:
Of politicians we are told to beware,
For they are all so full of hot air;
For instance, the diapers of Justin are as dry as a dustbin,
For, you see, he's the son of Pierre.
This legislation and this particular clause remind me of 1984. It can happen so easily, where you have listening in and where government can do what it wishes to do when it believes it to be in the public interest and necessary for the public good. That clause is so loosy-goosy that any government in power can do whatever it may wish with it. Certainly, the committee must get down to hard facts and really tighten up that clause before we find ourselves in very serious trouble. That particular clause is coated with corruption; it is there. I think that unless that clause in the legislation is changed we will be changing the whole aspect of a free parliamentary system. The system will not last, and could not last, if that power is given.
We see what has happened in respect of our neighbour to the south with regard to both the Pentagon papers and the Watergate situations. I do not know how the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), having seen what has happened there, could codify it and make it possible for government to do it. I wonder whether they have read the legislation and have seen what it says. We object violently and point

the finger to our neighbour, but we should first look more deeply at our own backyard and criticize ourselves before we have the temerity to criticize our brother. We should take the mote from our own eyes.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the fact that this type of invasion of the rights of the people of this country must be stopped. This legislation is a step forward. There are many changes which must be made to it in the committee. I hope the necessary corrections will be accomplished.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is surprising in a country such as Canada that we should be speaking in the same breath about two things: first, the right of the individual liberty of the citizen and, second, the right of Big Brother to supervise this liberty and the extent of it. I am sure most Canadians, no matter what walk of life they come from or what part of Canada they live in, will agree that they have the right to privacy and that that right is probably their most fundamental right as human beings. With the loss of privacy one becomes no better than an animal in a cage in a zoo.
I was pleased to hear the reference of the previous speaker to the year 1984 as being an indication that he also agrees we will soon reach that stage where the ability of Big Brother to direct and influence the lives of every individual will be accepted. I object to the docility of the Canadian public in a number of fields, and this is one. The other one which bothers me very greatly is the invasion of privacy which takes place when a person is searched at an airport. I know why people are searched; I know that we are trying to provide a deterrent. But we are providing a deterrent for a very limited number of incidents where hijacking might take place.
At the same time, however, we allow people to sit in our airports and sell life insurance. Over the years this has been one of the major causes of disasters in the air. It has been violently opposed by all the people who work for the airlines. It is very easy to insure your wife and then send her on a trip with a small parcel containing a bomb. This is allowed, and we know it has been a big factor in air disasters. We allow it because it is a form of business, and we really cannot interfere with the large insurance companies! We search people and we know what we are searching for. However, a metal detector is used. Anyone in his right mind would not carry a hand grenade; he would have to have a mental problem before he would board an aircraft with a bag full of hand grenades. He would carry a plastic bomb which could be contained in a pocket or which could be carried in a number of ways. It certainly would not be detected by a metal detector. I do not believe most people would attempt to carry sophisticated weapons on board an aircraft. If so, we should be using a totally different approach for them.
No one becomes angry about being searched, or objects to it. No one will object when the day arrives when people are searched in a supermarket. They do not object because it happens very occasionally and usually does not happen to them. It is always somebody else who is involved, and that really does not matter. I suggest that if the government wishes to bring in a bill, such a bill should totally outlaw eavesdropping by electronic devices.
We made a great hullabaloo when we stopped hanging criminals in this country except in the case of murder of a
Protection of Privacy
policeman. But have we hanged any one who has murdered a policeman since that time? No. We wrote that provision in merely to satisfy the law enforcement people. Two sections are being written into this bill. One will allow the police to carry on surveillance activities against almost anyone. Then we cover that up by allowing the security people, who are a totally different group, to go to the attorney general of a province or to the Solicitor General federally and ask permission to carry on surveillance in the case of national or provincial espionage. That is window-dressing. The people who are responsible for security in this country do not need to ask the government for the right to exercise that kind of surveillance, because we have provided them with the necessary type of equipment and training and with that very elementary device whereby they can go to the Attorney General and ask for permission to use that kind of information.
This right would only be provided once. The Minister of National Defence would go to the Attorney General of Canada and say that the use of certain surveillance equipment was necessary in the interest of national security for the army, navy or air force and he would be allowed to use it. This would be a blanket authorization and it would be carried like warrants and carried by RCMP officers. Once they are given, they are given for an indefinite period. They can do all sorts of things under those warrants.
Most crooks would not be caught by the equipment that is being used today to bug a room, a telephone service or other equipment. If you think your telephone is being bugged or the room in which you are is being bugged, ask somebody to build you a small oscillator. It will cost perhaps $10. Anybody who is using a tape recorder to record a conversation in the room would find that the tape recorder cannot pick up the conversation if on the oscillator you use decibels higher than the human ear can hear. There will be nothing on that tape except a high pitched screech which will destroy everything that is being recorded.
You can get such a device for about $10-any kid can make you one. Children today have a high awareness of electronic devices and can not only dial long distance but place international calls through satellites and perform all sorts of manoeuvres, simply because they know something about the theory of sound, which is really what we are talking about when we refer to eavesdropping. The eavesdropping to which we refer is so elementary and unsophisticated that in my opinion it is not being used by many people.
The privacy that is being invaded and that has been mentioned by other people is not covered by this legislation. This is something for which every member of the House should have some responsibility. I am referring to the new kind of invasion of privacy which is taking place, in particular through the setting up of memory and data banks as well as credit banks and all the other types of data processing information centres which provide information on people from the cradle to the grave and is completely legal and of great value to the person who may be using it.

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) mentioned several instances, such as the espionage that is taking place in industry and the ability of smart, young engineers with initiative to use the communications system to tap information banks and obtain any kind of information in almost any part of the world illegally, and use it to make a huge profit. If you have the ability to enter into the memory bank of a large multinational corporation, then you really have the equivalent of the ability to print money. Incidentally, this is being done by many multinational corporations to obtain information on whether or not they should buy a company or play monopoly with other companies, with workers lives and with the very economics of a country.
The provisions of this bill do not cover this type of activity which is an invasion of privacy. If some credit agency states that you are a poor risk because when you were 20 years old you had a nervous breakdown while you were going through college, and if that information in a memory bank somewhere was made available, it might stop you from obtaining a loan or it might do something which happened in another country, namely, stop a young, progressive person from becoming the vice-president of one of the major political parties in that country.
That is the kind of invasion of privacy from which this government should be protecting us. I am referring to protection against the invasion of privacy in the industrial world and in various government agencies where the storing of information is taking place. It is getting to the stage where, if you have access to unemployment insurance data you will know a considerable amount about any person on whom information is stored in that data bank, information about where he works, how long he has worked, what his address is, how many kids he has, what his status is, etc. You would then have unlimited knowledge about him which I am sure he would not want you to have. That information would be available to you if you could invade the privacy of the data bank.
The government has not given any consideration to that matter in the bill before us. I have heard members refer to espionage. We have had only one case of espionage since I became a member, namely, the Spencer case. Would it not be a great thing for the Attorney General, working closely with officers of the Department of Justice who had already decided that here was a poor, harmless, dying man, to state the RCMP should be allowed to attach all the necessary listening devices and to harass him by listening in on his private conversations and following up any contacts that poor Mr. Spencer had. This is a beautiful case of espionage, the only one that has been made public!
In the United States there are two controls that would be available under this kind of legislation and are not available in Canada. In Canada, judges are appointed by the government, although I understand there are exceptions and on rare occasions advice is being given by law societies in the provinces which occasionally make recommendations, although very seldom. Often, defeated political candidates become judges. They are always people who have an obligation to the government and they are not really the kind of people whom you would want to entrust with the responsibility of granting a warrant.
It has always impressed me that when a man goes on strike he has very little chance of getting an injunction against the company involved, but as soon as he goes on strike it is very easy for the boss to see the judge and ask him for an injunction against such and such a union or such and such a plant. He gets that injunction almost invariably without any justification at all. This is true with search warrants. It has been true with regard to every invasion of the rights of workers in this country, Mr. Speaker. It has always been true so far as the workers are concerned but never, never, never applies to the management of the companies.
This reminds me of the will of God clause which is written into many labour and insurance contracts. As an individual, it always seems to me that God is never on my side in those contracts but is always on the side of the companies. This is true whether it be the case of a labour dispute or a dispute over an insurance policy. I think in the present instance God would always be on the side of the Department of Justice, never on my side, and I would be getting the short end of the stick.
In the United States, judges secure office in two ways. In the case of Supreme Court judges a recommendation is made to Congress. Congress has to approve the appointment of a Supreme Court judge. Who appoints such judges in Canada? It is the Minister of Justice. He is always coming before us and asking for the appointment of another three judges somewhere, and he appoints three of his friends. Invariably the appointments are made in that way.
In the United States there is a second way by which judges secure office, and that is by vote. I do not agree that it is a very good system but at least the public has some say in appointing a judge and some choice in getting rid of a judge. With respect to the Watergate case in the United States, why would anyone have any hesitation asking the approval of John Mitchell, the Attorney General responsible for the security of the nation, for permission to engage in wiretapping? Nixon, as President of the United States, represents the top security of the nation, and in such a case anything done to defend him, no matter what it is, would be in the interests of the nation. Therefore, he would go to John Mitchell, as he did or as someone did and ask about this matter. And then he fires them. He says, "I am above all of them. God is on my side. I don't have to resign, but the rest of you had better resign." Mr. Speaker, it could happen here very easily.
I can remember ministers of justice in this House not too long ago who were not the kind of people in whom the average citizen could put much faith. I also remember that a very short time ago we had a solicitor general who was so contemptuous of the representatives of the people that he would not allow us to visit the jails. Not only would he not let the public go in, but he would not let their representatives go in although that right was written into the law of this country for 100 years and was removed only because a former solicitor general said, "You won't need that. That is British law and it will always be there."
I do not think that the individual in this country will be protected by this legislation, but the police will be protect-
(Mr. Peters.]
May 7, 1973

ed with respect to something they already do. The police will not be any more effective against the Mafia or against anybody who is influential. I am not suggesting that a judge will not give authorization in such a case, but such people are also pretty sophisticated and I am sure they will take precautions against electronic surveillance devices. Such precautions are simple to take.
Progress in this whole field is taking place so rapidly that every time you visit an exhibition of such electronic equipment you find new devices that were not there when you visited it the previous year. The crooks know this and the police know it. There is not a heck of a lot of difference, in many cases, between organized crime and the police force. One is organized on one hand and the other is organized on the other hand, and they both play a real game. But, Mr. Speaker, that game should not affect the individual. The individual should not lose his right to privacy because of the game being played between the police and organized crime in this country.
It is the little guy who gets hurt, the guy who may be cheating 10 bucks or 20 bucks on his income tax. He is the guy who is going to get hurt here. The bootlegger is going to get hurt. The prostitute is going to get hurt. It is very easy to listen to their conversations. The Mounties don't get red ears; they don't mind listening into a conversation in somebody's bedroom. As I say, prostitutes can get hurt. I can see Jarvis Street, with all the mobile listening units. The old judge will be issuing the mobile unit licences, and they will be up and down Jarvis Street in Toronto without number. I can see the accidents taking place between these mobile units in Jarvis Street, and the same will be true of Craig Street in Montreal and of several other streets in that vicinity.

Well, Mr. Speaker, not even prostitution is organized in Timiskaming; it still remains a relatively unorganized operation, with everybody for themselves. I think the police will probably engage in the free enterprise system of getting a contact here and a contact there and getting some information here and some information there, so nothing in Timiskaming is really going to happen in that field. But I suggest that in other places the police will have a field day.
I have not heard anybody say anything about the other security agency that we have built up in this country, and I am not talking about S and I. Everybody knows about Security and Intelligence. Everybody knows what it does. It is a pretty open book. It handles normal security and intelligence connected with police matters. But now we have another agency. This other agency was set up by the government to look after the security of government against espionage. I do not know the name of one person in that agency. I have not heard that it has even reported to the responsible minister. I do not know if it has ever reported to a committee. I do not know any activity that it has investigated. I do not know if it operates in conjunction with the RCMP or not. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that agency, operating in the dark, may not be too far away from the CIA in the United States, and I would not be too surprised if there are a number of people in that agency who are also counteragents for the CIA.
Protection of Privacy
Also, I would suggest that, operating under the Attorney General of Canada, they will probably not have much difficulty in getting any type of sophisticated equipment approved by the Solicitor General and that they will not have much difficulty in operating in a pretty free and easy way, without any kind of protection for the public.
I am opposed to this kind of bill. I have no faith in the ability of our police force to police what are truly matters of security. I have seen them chase red herrings for 20 years. I have seen members of the RCMP at every major union meeting that I attended for ten years. I am well aware that they have attended university campuses in about the same haphazard manner. I am quite sure that their purpose there was to write voluminous reports on a number of people and that this was an invasion of privacy that was not justified in the realm of national security. I am sure it was an undue and unreasonable invasion of the privacy of young people, of the privacy of individuals, of the privacy of Canadians in general.
Mr. Speaker, every time there is a demonstration on Parliament Hill we see about one and a half times the number of the members of the press gallery out there taking pictures. Half of that number is press gallery members but the other half is always the same people; they always look the same-they carry their guns the same. They are the same people and they take pictures of the crowd from all angles and by telescopic lens from the tops of buildings across the street and from the top of this building. They have taken pictures of every crowd that has gathered in front of parliament for the last five or six years. If anyone doubts this they should ask themselves how they got those pictures when Mr. Kosygin was here. The same pictures of the same person were being taken at every demonstration in the United States, Toronto, Montreal and elsewhere.
When these pictures were matched it was found that the same guy had been at four or five of the rallies. The RCMP got this information because they are there taking pictures, keeping files and maintaining a record on everybody who attends every meeting. In my opinion, that is an invasion of privacy. Another example is when Mr. Nixon was here and pictures were taken of him. Who takes them? The RCMP takes them, or agents of the RCMP, and they keep a file. This makes things easy for the police. That might be an advantage in a police state. In some countries it is very easy, because when you go to town the first thing you do is not just look for a hotel but for the police station. You give your name, state your business, who you are going to see, how long you will be staying. This makes things very easy for the police, but it is not the kind of country we want to live in. Most of our citizens came to this country to get away from that sort of thing. They do not want Big Brother. Mr. Speaker, what we want is the very maximum right of liberty and of privacy for the individual.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
When you take that away for no reason at all, you are taking the right of the individual to be free. I believed that when we brought in the War Measures Act.

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
The things that took place under that act were a disgrace and an indication that government never operates on behalf of the people but only operates on behalf of government and the perpetuity of that government. That was a clear case where violent abuses took place because we developed a hysteria. If we again develop a hysteria against organized crime and allow invasion of privacy, again the individual loses.
Mr. Speaker, every time I go the airport I am shocked, concerned and saddened to see people submitting, like sheep, to being searched. I do not care if they take the plane to Cuba. We have a non-scheduled flight every day from Halifax, or perhaps two flights a day. If Air Canada flies me there, I would like them to keep me in a hotel for four or five days so that I could have a holiday, and then bring me back. I am not concerned, either, about the person who hijacks the plane to some place other than Cuba but I am concerned about the nut who gets on the airplane and wants to destroy it. If anyone wants to destroy an airplane flying 50,000 feet above the ocean, all he has to do is kick out a window. Seat belts would make no difference; the pressure on every person would be about four or five tons and the plane would crash. There is no need for a bomb; everybody knows that. The person to be worried about is the one who is going to steal the airplane and hold it to ransom.
I am willing to take the risk of somebody hijacking the plane. Well, nobody is going to hijack the one that goes to northern Quebec, so I am fairly safe; nor is anybody going to hijack the one that my colleague uses to go to Val d'Or, Rouyn, Earlton, North Bay or Toronto. However, Mr. Speaker, I am concerned that people are searched and that their luggage is searched on the strength that something has happened once or twice.
If you get on a bus and the bus has an accident, they do not then give the driver a breathalyzer test every time, nor do they check the tires every time. The Ontario Northland is recapping tires on its buses six times. One caused an accident and killed many people not long ago. No commercial vehicle has tires that are recapped more than three times. Well, we ride that bus and do not search it or do some of the things that we should for our own protection, but we docilely let the police or security people search us. They have the right, as well, to go before a judge and get the authority to wiretap.
Mr. Speaker, nobody has even suggested that we have an ombudsman to represent the public as the Auditor General does in regard to public accounts. The minister will get the file. But the minister was foolish enough to take on such things as the Wheat Board as well as the Department of Justice, so he is not going to have time to read about all the telephone calls that have been made and make a decision on whether the judge should allow it or not. A third party is not even allowed to represent the individual.
I am violently opposed to the invasion of privacy that we, as Members of Parliament, are allowing for no reason. If there were a demonstrated need for this, then maybe we should consider it. I think this government should be introducing a bill to eliminate the right to wiretapping with rare exceptions, those exceptions to be stringently policed. The police force should not be allowed to get a

search warrant or injunction, but the individual's privacy should be retained at all costs.
We should stir the people of this country to object to the invasion of privacy, to object to the benefit control officers of the UIC asking the personal questions they do. Once you have been asked all those questions, Mr. Speaker, once somebody listens to your telephone conversations, once you no longer have privacy in your own home, then you are no longer master in your own house and you have really lost a great deal of your individuality; you become close to being an animal. That animal will be 1984 and it will be Big Brother who will make the decision for you. You will be trained to like it, accept it and even to appreciate it.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to hear my hon. friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) speak of the new philosophy of the New Democratic Party. He suggested the government acts only on behalf of the government. I am most impressed if that is that party's position in dealing with regulatory legislation. Presumably, those members will now be voting with my party, the party of freedom, the party that is concerned with individual liberty. It is in that respect that I wish to make some remarks tonight.
The matter of electronic snooping has been raised in the press in the last few weeks in connection with the Watergate affair in the United States. I commend the minister for bringing this matter to the attention of this House at this time. The people of this country are totally unhappy over the use of bugging or electronic snooping devices. They have no reason to wish for this kind of activity and are most emphatically in favour of laws protecting privacy.
If this bill contained only section 178.1 and 178.11 and nothing else, I would commend it entirely to this House and say it is a terrific piece of legislation. Under those two sections, conviction for electronic snooping brings a penalty of up to five years in jail. Electronic snooping is pretty clearly prohibited. Nevertheless, the bill goes on to authorize electronic snooping not only on the part of officers of the Crown but, as pointed out by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Morgan), by private and public telephone and telecommunication companies. The authorization of such invasion of privacy leaves a great deal to be desired and the entire matter must be examined seriously in committee.
It is surprising that the government continues to put forward police state type electronic snooping measures as proposed in this legislation. This is the third time a bill like this has been before the House and, presumably, this bill will go to committee for the third time. Each time provision has been made whereby officers of the Crown and others will be entitled, under certain conditions, to eavesdrop on every bit of private conversation that you and I, Mr. Speaker, may have. It is in that respect also that I wish to address the House tonight.
Not only is the eavesdropping of the government under certain conditions permitted; all of a sudden the results of this eavesdropping will now become legitimate evidence in court. According to section 178.14, if an ex parte
May 7, 1973

application is granted by a judge of the superior court and eavesdropping is undertaken, the evidence in connection with the eavesdropping can be introduced in court and is to be treated as proper and valid evidence. This is an amazing extension of the laws of evidence as relating to courts. All of a sudden the private conversation in someone's living room, the private conversation in someone's office, say in the Confederation Building between members of this House, or the private conversation over a telephone may become evidence. If a constituent says over the telephone that the Prime Minister should drop dead, that statement may be treated in court as evidence if there is a charge of espionage or something like that.
What will happen, Mr. Speaker? Sure, the tape will be given to the accused; the accused will have access to that information. But the tape will be produced in court and entered as evidence and what was said will be loud and clear, almost like a picture. The court and jury, if there is a jury, will have the right to hear that kind of evidence. Such evidence will not have been obtained by someone directly seeing the subject; it will not be direct evidence given by someone who heard somebody else say something. It will be the evidence of a machine. The machine will have heard something said. The machine will be played in court, and what is recorded may lead to a conviction. That is the kind of thing authorized under this bill. That is a serious extension of the law of evidence, and a very serious infringement of liberty. That is the kind of thing we find in this bill. Therefore, this bill is not properly named as clause 1 says-"This act may be cited as the protection of privacy act." Here is a bill that legitimizes wiretapping evidence. That is a serious provision that will have to be expunged from the bill in committee.
May I deal with the next subject. Authority to conduct this kind of invasion of privacy is to be obtained by way of ex parte application to the court. Every lawyer who has practised law knows that you always go to a friendly judge if you want a friendly order. Really, the friendly judge is always there as my hon. friend from Timiskaming pointed out. I have lots of faith in our judiciary, I have practised law and have gone to friendly judges on behalf of my clients to get friendly orders. There is really not too much difficulty in getting such an order if you want one. Now there are to be ex parte applications for permission to bug.
Under this government we have seen the proliferation of all sorts of ex parte applications. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), who I see is here, gets ex parte orders every day to garnishee citizens' wages of this country because they happen to have been overpaid by his department in the matter of unemployment insurance. All of a sudden people find that their bank account is lighter by a couple of hundred dollars or so because the minister has obtained an ex parte order of garnishment. Those are the kinds of ex parte orders I am talking about. You never find out about them until they hit you.
The same holds true for the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury). If he wants to make a seizure because you have not paid your income tax, the minister obtains an ex parte order and makes an ex parte seizure. This is done all of a sudden. There is no due process of law here;
Protection of Privacy
there is an ex parte order and seizure. That is the kind of thing that is creeping into our statutes. There is an ex parte order and that is it. And this bill is supposed to protect the rights of the citizen!
I referred to the kinds of orders the Minister of Manpower and Immigration obtains to garnishee people's wages. I dealt with one such order the other day involving a constituent who had already gone bankrupt. The minister's department had been advised of the bankruptcy yet the minister authorized that ex parte garnishee and it went through. Even though I told the minister that the constituent had gone bankrupt, the minister said, "I have a court order, old boy, and I would garnishee him anyway." That is the kind of attitude that prevails under these kinds of ex parte proceedings. Provision is made for them in other statutes, and there is no reason to believe it will not happen under this statute.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext: And that is the minister who has unlimited access to our national bank account.

subsubtopic: CREATION OF OFFENCES RELATED TO INTERCEPTION OF PRIVATE COMMUNICATIONS BY CERTAIN DEVICES
speechtext:
Yes, he has unlimited access. It would not be so bad if the orders had to be obtained by the minister. However, from looking at this statute we find that the attorneys general of the provinces, the Solicitor General of Canada or their agents-and that could be a corporal in the RCMP or a police constable in Mississauga-could obtain, on an ex parte order from some judge somewhere, the right to bug, wiretap and do all sorts of things. It is not the minister, but the minister's agent. Almost any person could be the minister's agent. This provision is far too loose. It has far too wide an application and puts far too wide a right in the hands of the Crown or its servants. The whole matter of delegation must be looked at. There should be no right of delegation in this serious invasion of the privacy and rights of individuals.
The bill further states that you do not even need a court application. All you need is the minister's agent, his police office, to think that maybe it is a matter of urgency and for a 36-hour period, without limitation, they can go in and wiretap on their own. They do not even need an order. For 36 hours they are foot-loose and fancy free. Eventually they may get an order, but they may not. They may decide to wiretap my friend here, my friend there or any person in my constituency for any reason at all. They do not have to report. They do not have to justify their activities.
I wish to deal further with this ex parte order. Having obtained the ex parte order, does the minister or the police have to make the details of the ex parte order public knowledge? Not on your life. The whole system can be buried. The file remains sealed until it is destroyed. The accused who is charged as a result of an improperly obtained ex parte order has no right to cross-examine the grounds on which the order was obtained in the first place. The evidence obtained against him is not open to cross-examination. The fact that it was obtained without the right to have it in the first place, without the right of being open to examination or cross-examination, is used against him.

May 7, 1973
Protection of Privacy
Under section 178(2)(i) we find that on proof of conviction or illegal wiretapping the government of Canada, without the right to go into property and civil rights, declares a damage suit for $5,000. Surely a claim for punitive damages, which is a tort, should not be set out in the Criminal Code. After all, the Criminal Code should not set out grounds for civil damage or even limitations on grounds for civil damage. This is clearly a matter within the competence of the provinces. This section should be removed from the statute. If a person is aggrieved by the improper use of wiretapping and sues someone for that, there is no reason why the person so aggrieved should have his damages limited to $5,000 by the Parliament of Canada. The whole question of damage and civil litigation is a matter within the competence of the provinces of this country. It is not a matter of competence of the federal parliament. On that basis, this section must be removed from the statute.
There are a lot of things said by people on the telephone and otherwise. Things are sometimes said when they should not be said. Things are sometimes said in a way they should not be said. As a politician, I know that. Your Honour also knows it. Loose comments are made. Surely, loose comments made by people over the telephone and picked up as a result of the authority given to the police office to bug the telephone or otherwise should not be used as evidence in a court of law. Just because someone says he is going to do something that is possibly of a seditious nature, it should not be used in evidence against that person just because it was said in private.
This whole question must be looked at, and looked at seriously. It is very easy for politicians to talk about fixing a nomination. It is very easy for people to talk over the phone about fixing a horse race. Because it was very easy for my constituent, a middle-aged lady, to talk about getting rid of the Prime Minister, this idle chatter should not be used as evidence against her in a court of law. That is the kind of authority that is being given by this parliament as a result of this bill.
There is one other thing I would like to say before Your Honour calls it ten o'clock. I wish to make this point very clear. Evidence is taken on the quiet without any person understanding that it is being taken from him. It is taken secretively without his having any understanding of what is happening. All of a sudden it is used against him. This is totally against our concept of British justice. On that basis, the clauses in this bill authorizing electronic snooping must be deleted.

subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL-PROPOSED OTTAWA-HULL RAPID TRANSIT-POSITION OF FEDERAL GOVERNMENT RESPECTING CONTRIBUTION TO COST
NATIONAL CAPITAL-PROPOSED OTTAWA-HULL RAPID TRANSIT-POSITION OF FEDERAL GOVERNMENT RESPECTING CONTRIBUTION TO COST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 5 last, as recorded at page 1883 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) a question the text of which appears on that page. The question relates to the necessity of a financial contribution, which I and many others have said is the responsibility of the federal government, toward the development of a rapid transit system in the national capital.
On January 30 the province of Ontario made an announcement wherein it stated it was prepared to put up a large sum of money toward the cost of developing a system of rapid transit for the Ontario side of the national capital area. At that time it invited participation by the Government of Canada. Since then, neither the government nor the National Capital Commission has made any commitment whatsoever to sharing in this type of development although I am sure there have been discussions with respect to it.
The important thing, however, was the minister's answer. Apart from the fact that he jumped to the conclusion I was assuming something that I was not, he evaded the direct question and replied that in effect there would be no contribution until a co-operative arrangement had been arrived at within the whole of the national capital region, that is, on both sides of the river, in Quebec as well as Ontario. No one quarrels with the concept that there should be development on both sides of the Ottawa River and that both sides ought to develop space. On the other hand, no one can realistically believe that what is desirable is always possible or that differences in attitudes and needs and states of readiness can be ignored.
A commitment has been made, however, by the province of Ontario which will benefit the Ontario side. A regional transport authority has been established throughout the regional municipality of Ottawa, or Ottawa-Carleton. There has long been a need for rapid transit. An invitation to the federal government to make a contribution has been made. This invitation ought to be answered now. It ought to be answered in the affirmative. It ought to have been answered in the affirmative a long time ago. It is neither fair nor reasonable that those who want such a service now should have that service delayed while they wait for another jurisdiction. I have no hesitation in saying that the reasons for delay on the part of the other jurisdictions may be reasonable. None the less, this delay should not penalize most who reside in the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton.
On this side of the river there are now half a million people who require rapid transit. They live in the capital of Canada. They live in an age when we should be doing our best to improve our city. The national capital ought to
May 7, 1973

be a model for all forms of services which municipalities supply. Yet in the field of transportation we still live in a dark age. The answer is obviously rapid transit. In this age, the traditional bus service will not do.
Having said this, I want to add that no doubt the federal government is experiencing difficulties in co-ordination at this time; there are two municipal jurisdictions, two provincial jurisdictions and the federal government is in the middle. This situation ought to raise, not obstacles but rather challenges for the federal government. Perhaps the time has come for us to constitute the parliamentary committee which has been talked about in the newspapers and in this House from time to time, and ask it to examine the structure and the place of the National Capital Commission. In doing this, perhaps we should consider whether the time has not come for the new types of municipalities, the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton on the one hand and Outaouais municipality on the other, to be represented on the National Capital Commission.
Perhaps we should seek to determine the real place of the federal government in such an arrangement. Perhaps we ought not to turn our backs on the possibility that there may be some good come of local government involvement at the policy level, and that more could be done in the national capital than the commission's traditional role of tending flowerbeds and building highways- that its real role with respect to development and planning might be recognized by local participation. Perhaps we should take advantage of these new municipal structures so that there could be co-ordination at the policy level between the municipal governments and the National Capital Commission. Perhaps we ought to say that the National Capital Commission has a place on a regional transportation body or bodies which affect both sides of the river. Perhaps the question, the answer to which I sought on March 5, might be answered in that way.
I hope that when the parliamentary secretary rises he will announce that the government does, indeed, intend to go ahead now and act with respect to that part of the national capital area which has made a request for a federal contribution to the development of a modern rapid transit system in that part of the national capital area which has shown itself ready and able to absorb it.
The challenges that face the national capital area have been too long characterized as difficulties. My respectful submission is that this government has not been active enough in meeting the challenges. One of the great challenges it must meet in this area is the challenge before it of providing, on this side at least in the beginning, perhaps as an example to the other side, a modern, up to date and thoroughly sound rapid transit system so that we will not forever become the victim of the automobile and the expensive highways which are necessary for its maintenance.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL-PROPOSED OTTAWA-HULL RAPID TRANSIT-POSITION OF FEDERAL GOVERNMENT RESPECTING CONTRIBUTION TO COST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been asked by my colleague, the hon. member for Laprai-rie (Mr. Watson), the parliamentary secretary in this area, to present this reply.
The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) asked whether, in the event that one or other of the
Adjournment Debate
provincial governments is not prepared to participate in the conditions necessary to establish rapid transit to serve the national capital region, the federal government would deal separately with one of these governments in the granting of funds for a system on only one side of the Ottawa River.
The minister is not prepared at this time to accept the premises of the question. Indeed, there is considerable evidence that there is sufficient understanding of the necessity for rapid transit for the national capital region on a truly regional basis to include both sides of the Ottawa River and to be an integral part of a balanced transportation network for the whole region.
In support of this I would point out that the Premier of Ontario has made public statements inviting the co-operation of both the federal government and the province of Quebec in dealing with transit proposals for the national capital region which have been recently announced by his government. Moreover, it is also evident that the province of Quebec is initiating steps dealing with transit and is making a considerable effort to overcome the disparity which now exists between the two provinces in the national capital.
Consequently, the minister is satisfied that in the case of both provinces there is an appreciation of the necessity to plan and implement rapid transit on a regional basis and in a co-operative manner with the federal government. I am sure, therefore, there is agreement on the importance of rapid transit in the national capital region to all three senior governments, as well as to the municipalities to be served on both sides of the Ottawa River, and that these governments are therefore willing to work together on this matter.
This seems to be the appropriate time to seek a meeting to discuss public transit and transportation in the region with the other senior levels of government. To this end the minister is now making arrangements for a meeting with representatives of Ontario and Quebec at which we expect a very co-operative approach to be taken. In due course the minister will undoubtedly be reporting further to the House.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-ADEQUACY OF TOFINO LIFEBOAT STATION SERVICE IN LIGHT OF DROWNINGS
TRANSPORT-ADEQUACY OF TOFINO LIFEBOAT STATION SERVICE IN LIGHT OF DROWNINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) a question regarding the very unfortunate incident which happened last Wednesday, May 2, near Tofino on the west coast of Vancouver Island. At 2 a.m. four persons were making their way in a small boat, a dug-out canoe, to the Opitsat Indian reserve and the boat capsized. Fortunately, Mr. Walter Arnett, who was a member of the lifeboat crew, heard the shouting and sent out an alarm. Mr. John Shaw launched a rubber boat within four minutes of hearing the alarm and managed to rescue Mr. Henry Williams. Someone on the wharf rescued Mrs. David Henry Williams. Within 15 minutes of the rubber boat being launched, the lifeboat was launched and scoured the area but was unable to find the other two. As a result, David Henry Williams, age 33, and Mrs. Martha Martin, age 73, were drowned.

May 7, 1973
Adjournment Debate
I did not raise this matter with a view to criticizing the crew of the lifeboat station; not at all. If they were able to launch a rubber boat within four minutes and launch a lifeboat within 15 minutes of hearing the alarm, I think they deserve every commendation. I raise the matter because there is a growing feeling among people on the Pacific coast that the curtailment of the staff of the various lifeboat stations has contributed to many of the losses of life at sea in recent years.
When one considers that this lifeboat crew is on duty from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., seven days a week, and on call all the rest of the time 24 hours a day, seven days a week, one realizes it is virtually impossible to expect that these men can be found by telephone message from the marine radio station at any hour of the day or night. They go out sometimes to visit friends, to go to church, to visit the beer parlour or somewhere else. It is only between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. that persons are actually at the lifeboat station. For the remainder of the time the safety of people at sea is dependent upon someone being able to find the persons who are on call but are not really on duty.
I do not believe it was good economy when some time ago the department reduced the staff of these lifeboat stations. The men who go down to the sea in ships and do business in deep water have a right to better protection than that which they are being given. It is not merely a matter of these four persons who were making their way to the Indian reserve: there are fishing fleets 25 or 30 miles out to sea and any one of them could capsize or be involved in a collision.
There is a need for two things. There is need for a modern, up to date ship-to-shore radio service and lifeboat station crews available at all times to launch a boat and go to the rescue of those whose ship has been wrecked or destroyed. I do not raise this matter to either embarrass the minister or find fault with the lifeboat crew, who apparently in this particular instance acted with commendable speed and energy. My purpose in raising the matter is to ask the government, through the Minister of Transport, to look into this situation to see if the paring of the staff of the lifeboat stations has resulted in a situation in which people's lives are in jeopardy.
When I ask for an investigation, I do not mean public servants investigating themselves. I mean someone from the minister's office or persons familiar with lifeboat operations and coastguard services who would look into this matter. They should be people who are not intimately connected with the operation. It should certainly not be done by someone from the Treasury Board to see whether there could be a saving. This is not a case of saving dollars but, rather, of saving lives. This is what I am interested in.
I ask the minister, through the minister's parliamentary secretary, if the department will look into this question of lifeboat stations to see whether men could be on duty on three shifts of eight hours each, which would mean that they would be there and available to meet any mishap. I know some steps are being taken toward this end, but they have been very slow. There needs to be a tremendous improvement in order to achieve some radio service, particularly the ship-to-shore radio service on the Pacific coast. With those two things, adequate lifeboat

crews and up to date radio communication, I think we could reduce the loss of life that has been all too common in recent years on the Pacific coast.

speakeroldname: Mr. loseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSPORT-ADEQUACY OF TOFINO LIFEBOAT STATION SERVICE IN LIGHT OF DROWNINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the hon. member that I have taken careful note of the comments he has made, of his concern and of the various other points that he outlined. At the same time, I would like to say to him, on behalf of the department, that from our review of the whole operation there is no doubt in our minds that a sufficient crew is manning the station.
In order to confirm this opinion it should be noted that it was one of the members of our lifeboat crew who first became aware of the emergency and put the rescue operation in action, which included the launching of the rubber boat and the rescue, and the further launching of the larger lifeboat, both of which took place in extremely short periods of time. Additional staff would not conceivably have improved the speed with which this whole operation was carried out.
It must also be borne in mind that all this took place during the hours of darkness. A special investigation team was sent to the scene of this unfortunate incident to look into all details relating to it. The investigation is still under way.

subtopic: INFORMATION-POSSIBILITY OF USE OF RETAIL CREDIT CORPORATION BY DEPARTMENTS TO OBTAIN INFORMATION
INFORMATION-POSSIBILITY OF USE OF RETAIL CREDIT CORPORATION BY DEPARTMENTS TO OBTAIN INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a day when the right to privacy is being discussed in the House, and indeed throughout Canada and the United States, it is appropriate to consider whether the government's own house is in order. One of the more reprehensible types of invasion of privacy is the surreptitious investigation of persons by governments through the use of commercial credit agencies whose computer-stored data is often lacking in truth if not in substance.
On March 6 of this year I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) if he would advise whether any department of the federal government is a client of the Retail Credit Corporation or Company, or of any other commercial reporting agency and, if so, does it use the information received for purposes other than as an employer? My question was prompted by the following information which has been brought to my attention. The first information is that there is in existence an up to date, eleven-page manual of the Retail Credit Company called "Retail Credit Managers' Manual". It is my understanding that this is a confidential document which is not distributed to the public. Moreover, this manual contains words to the following effect under the heading "General Policies of the Retail Credit Company":
The company operates with the federal authorities in the United States and Canada. Requests usually come from the RCMP and other federal departments in Canada.
These departments have the right of subpoena and we try to co-operate with them. Any unjustifiable demands should be submitted to the company's legal department in Atlanta.
The passage to which I refer concludes by saying:
May 7, 1973

You should realize that the company's information is only hearsay and is not guaranteed.
That is from the "Retail Credit Manager's Manual," which is an up to date manual used by retail credit managers in the United States and Canada. In conclusion, I would refer to some statistics and a comment in the report of the task force on privacy and computers which was tabled in the House earlier this year. That report states at page 63:
Retail Credit of Canada, a subsidiary of the Retail Credit Corporation of Atlanta, Georgia, which is primarily an investigative credit bureau, has been diversifying into in-file operations. Approximately 30 per cent of the in-file business in Canada is now under its control.
In light of the information which I have laid before the House, I would appreciate it if the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) would provide a full and complete answer to the question which I have raised, in the context of the factual information and the resulting concerns arising therefrom.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: INFORMATION-POSSIBILITY OF USE OF RETAIL CREDIT CORPORATION BY DEPARTMENTS TO OBTAIN INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I cannot give the hon. gentleman the kind of assurances that perhaps he would like. I gather he would want to have assurance that no one in the government's employ has anything whatsoever to do with the Retail Credit Corporation or the Retail Credit Company of Canada. However, I can say that so far as the Treasury Board is concerned no directive, no instruction and no advice has ever been issued by that body enjoining departments to make use of this kind of service for any governmental purpose, and there have been no departments, to my knowledge, that have made use of the services of this corporation.
I am advised by the Public Service Commission that they have not, and do not intend to make use of the services of this particular corporation, either to obtain character references or, indeed, measurements of so-called credit worthiness when it comes to the matter of the recruiting of people or their appointment to the public service. So both the two control agencies at least do not make use of the facilities offered by this company themselves, nor have they given any advice or instruction to other government departments that they should use them.
